title: very optimistically early damage report | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "upperbaygardener", "author_name": "UpperBayGardener (zone 7)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/upperbaygardener", "date": "2022-02-01", "text": "We had 8.8F, and a long spell below 10F, a few weeks ago, and more recently 7.7F a few nights ago.  For all my winters in the past 16 years, that's pretty average, although I would say It's infrequent to go below 10F without the benefit of snow cover which was the case both of these times.  (well maybe 1.5 inches for the 7.7F, but that would barely count it seems.  Based on the fact York Co PA was warmer that night, it probably just made me colder than I would have been w/o snow cover...some places on the eastern shore of MD went < 0F because of their heavy snow cover in the latest nor'easter) My studies of winter climatology shows if we haven't been super cold by end of January, it's very unlikely there will be a turn for the worse.  But it can happen, there was a mid Feb. freeze at some point in the 90s IIRC, after a mild winter.  Knock on wood!  The start of the last week of February is when I truly feel out of the woods, so, jumping the gun just a bit. Anyhow... Most exciting is that a Eucalyptus delegatensis I collected myself from the last I found before the switchover to snow gums above 4400' or so appears almost totally undamaged.  Granted, I did give it a little wind screen, and it has protection from the dreaded winter morning sun.  But this is one that Ian Barclay, about as close to an expert on the PNW hardiness of gum trees as you are likely to find, said 'hadn't been very hardy at all' in the PNW.  Well, 7.7F is cold for the PNW.  So, that's encouraging.  I notice on both this E. and E. neglecta, its the very oldest foliage that burns.  The apparently new growth, even very tiny leaves at the branchlet tips, is totally intact. Less promising is Cinnamomum porrectum AKA C. parthenxylon.   Sold thusly by Cistus:  https://plantlust.com/plants/27895/cinnamomum-porrectum/ Dave Parks of Camellia Forest dryly commented \"that was the one that wasn't hardy for us\".  So, perhaps a lost cause, although TBH it doesn't look as bad as a C. wilsonii that was totally killed by a milder winter a few years ago.   It defoliated, but not as quickly.  Here's a discussion of these exotic trees I contributed to on another forum: https://growingontheedge.net/viewtopic.php?p=124558 The good news is a huge Cinnamomum japonicum in East Texas at SFASU survived -4F/-20C in the TX mega freeze.  So it gives me hope for that species, although I may not have the same clone as they do.  If you look at the overall mildness of their winters, -4F is potentially more destructive down there because Asian BLEs may not be in complete dormancy.  (although, also, potentially less for other reasons) Phormium 'Lake Te Anu'.  One of the only single-digit freezes it's had without snow cover.  Looking pretty good with just a bit of outer leaf burning.   This is a green selection from what was thought to be a cold part of NZ, although a horticulturalist I met at Christchurch Botanical Garden dismissed the notion that Lake Te Anu was especially cold.  I also have another clone i collected in Ophir, the coldest town in NZ by some estimates.  That one is bronzy and now that I've divided it, I will by trying it in the garden, too. A few other interesting items: Metapanax davidii...slight boiled cabbage look, but I think it's ok. Rhodoleia henryi 'Scarlet Bells' - looks OK! Eurya 'Moutiers' - just fine Trachycarpus planted in a SW facing alcove- just fine \"Zone 8\" Mahonia hybrid with gigantic leaves, bred at Bloedel and sold by Far Reaches - OK so far.  Has 100% protection from winter morning sun tho. UPDATE: just took closer look at this...maybe about 5-8% burning of the least hardened foliage...so the 'zone 8' classifications of these was probably reasonable.  I can't remember what the species were but the make up suggested it would be more tender than the typical M. x medias discussed next.  UPDATE pt 2 - found it: https://www.farreachesfarm.com/Mahonia-duclouxiana-x-M-japonica-p/p4537.htm Mahonia 'Arthur Menzies' - small planted last spring - just fine Mahonia 'Buckland' - just fine of course, huge plant now pushing 8', flower buds not killed yet apparently Erica terminalis 'Thelma Woolner' - bravely planted in late fall, but doing just fine.  This is the hardiest 'tree heath' but I have found almost all Ericas to be somewhat temperamental.  (and that includes a girl with that name I used to know har har har)   I have a whole emerging theory about the 'trick' to growing fine rooted Ericacaeae in my climate, but I'll go into it another time. Erythrina flabelliformis - to the extant you can tell, still ok.  (tip of \"bulb\" pectinate and looking like it did at end of growing season) Camellias:  all established ones just fine of course... new planted 'Robiraki' hanging in there same for a C. cuspidata alas, a 'Peacock'  (Kujaku) Camellia looks very unhappy.  Maybe that clone just isn't very hardy.  Hoping it recovers in spring. lastly: Magnolia skinneriana - extra hardy clone from somewhere  - fine, just a bit of singeing on the most sun exposed leaves. If it doesn't deep freeze again, I suspect it will bloom just fine Magnolia dianica or whatever they are calling it these days - same, it seems to be be hardy to about 5F Magnolia 'Frosty Pale Purple'  (M. figo var. skinneriana x figo var. crassipes) - almost 100%, leaves have a slight boiled cabbage look but I am sure it's nothing to worry about", "images": []}

title: Has anyone done a renovation on a Monocrete (Concrete wall) house? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "mark-wan58", "author_name": "Mark", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mark-wan58", "date": "2022-02-01", "text": "Hi there, My building and pest inspector has just informed me that the walls of a prospective purchase are made out of concrete. Looks to be a process designed to produce houses cheaply and quickly back in the 1950s https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monocrete_construction Has anyone ever had experience renovating one of these 1950s post-war houses? I'm particularly worried about how much it will cost to do a remodel and just general electrical work. Regards, Mark", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "compass-kitchens-pfvwau-pf~94857597", "author_name": "Compass Kitchens", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/kitchen-designers-and-remodelers/compass-kitchens-pfvwau-pf~94857597", "date": "2022-02-05", "text": "Hello Mark,  if the interior walls are plastered then to add electrical wiring and plumbing will be exactly the same process as if you home was brick construction with plastered interiors. Cost would also be the same as the trenching and re-flushing will be the same process. If your concrete internal walls are exposed however (same as in modern rammed earth walls or precast concrete walls today) then you would have to consider three options as to how to add electrical or plumbing lines and these would also have different costs depending on what you do. One option would be again to trench these in, and then cement over the trench when finished, however this would leave an obvious scar on the walls wherever the trenching is done. The other option would be to trench and then fill as-well-as then plaster over the entire wall that was effected; changing the exposed concrete appearance to a plastered appearance ready to paint. (instead of plastering you could alternatively wall-paper or use some other type of covering. The other option would be to run cable inside Trunking which is fixed and left exposed on the face of your walls, where this is often done in industrial style interior fit-outs and is also done in some heritage buildings. These really depend on what your walls are, how they have been finished already, and what you want them to look like when you finish renovating.       Hope this helps, Malcolm.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/d302d95001fe3a83_1076-w240-h242-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/5ea2f33401fe3a85_1077-w240-h159-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/0742e20801fe3a85_1078-w240-h321-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

title: Help with choice between stucco and Hardie board in Northern CA | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-432900512", "author_name": "Amy R", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-432900512", "date": "2022-02-01", "text": "Hello - My community is rebuiding three houses after losing nine to wildfire in 2020. We are trying to balance fire safety with the extremely high construction costs in Sonoma County. For permitting, we need to make a choice ASAP between stucco and Hardie board and are feeling stuck. Does anyone have experience with these materials in this climate - we are at 1500' so it gets very hot and dry in the summer, and alternates between thick fog, heavy rain, and sunshine in the winter.  And obviously there are more and more fires \u2639\ufe0f Other questions: How long do you think we could go before repainting a Hardie exterior? Is stucco an okay choice for earthquake country? Does anyone have any experience adding a layer of rockwool - for insulation and fire protection - under exterior siding of either material? Thank you!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kudzu9", "author_name": "kudzu9", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kudzu9", "date": "2022-02-01", "text": "I have Hardie board on my home in the Pacific NW. It's not as hot as you are in the summer, but there is more rain in the winter. We re-painted for the first time after about 15 years; but that was because we wanted to change the color, not because it had deteriorated or faded badly.  As someone who is also in earthquake country, I would prefer a wood frame house covered in Hardie board/plank, rather than a stucco house which I would see as prone to cracking if their was a significant earthquake. My thought is that rockwool would be a decent choice for insulating, but I don't think it is going to do a significantly better job of fire protection: if the flames are intense enough that the rockwool is a last ditch protective barrier, your house is probably pretty much destroyed anyway, and, once the exterior is breached, the rockwool would probably just spill out of the wall cavities. Buy four of the cheapest white muslin twin flat sheets you can find.  (Walmart used to sell flats and fitteds separately, but I don't know if they still do.)  Sheets are long enough to go floor to ceiling and they come with nice wide hems already sewn on one end.  Hold them up against the rods so the wide hem just clears the floor and mark on the other end where the top of the rod is.  Turn that end down that amount (narrow hem and all) and sew across to make a rod pocket.  (You can do two rows of stitching a little more than the rod width apart if you would like a ruffle at the top, above the rod. main_question: {"author_id": "ambloved", "author_name": "ann beck 8a ruralish WA", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ambloved", "date": "2022-02-01", "text": "I read somewhere that you can't propagate roses in early spring.  Is that true? For instance, if I took cuttings of my dormant roses now brought them inside for rooting, would they just leaf out and not root?  If I get cuttings from a friend in So Cal that have already bloomed, will it root for me indoors in winter? other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "erasmus-gw", "author_name": "erasmus_gw", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/erasmus-gw", "date": "2022-02-01", "text": "I am in zone 7a, NC,  so colder than where you are.   I used to root them mainly after they bloomed in spring,  and all summer into fall.   Now I also take cuttings in winter and many root.   I do have a plastic hoop house thing for a bit of protection during the  cold.  Some varieties seem to root better in cold temps. One OGR person who vistited me said February is the best month to root OGR's so I will be taking cuttings very soon if not today.   I worry a little about whether it will cause the parent  plant to put on new growth too soon but so far it really hasn't  been a problem.  For your own dormant cuttings I'd just try to root them outdoors.  You might be right that if you brought them indoors they'd leaf out,  not put out roots. You might want to tie loops at the ends if using a string. OR, Drop a piece of wood, plastic container, or other item(s) into the bottom of the pot so the actual pot is stable and the rim of the plant's pot sits just high enough over the rim of the cache pot to get a grip on it with your fingers. OR, Melt 2 holes on the actual pot with a hot nail held with pliers. Fashion 2 hooks from pieces of wire. Slip the hooks through the holes and lift. Fungal spores need a continual source of moisture over varying periods to activate.  This is the disease tetrahedron. All 4 of the requirements must be met for a pathogen to infect the plant. When you water, be sure the entire soil column has been moistened and at least 20% of the entire volume of water used during the session exits the drain hole. title: Choosing a pot size for pepper plants? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "katyajini", "author_name": "katyajini", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/katyajini", "date": "2022-02-01", "text": "Early on I found just about every vegetable I wanted to grow grew so much better in the ground  that I never tried to grow in pots anymore and have almost no experience in container gardening. Now I am seeing pepper plants growing just brilliantly in pots in peoples gardens, decks and balconies. I would like to try to grow a few peppers in pots this season.\ud83d\ude01 This is what I gathered.   Keeping in mind the mature size of the specific pepper plant, you can choose bigger and bigger pots to get a bigger plant and more peppers...But the bigger the pot size the longer the plant's roots will take to fill the soil volume.  Until the roots, more or less, fill the soil the plant will not put on any significant shoot growth and fruit set.  So you effectively delay fruit set and get a smaller harvest if you dont have a long enough growing season when you choose a *big* pot. Is this true?  Will you delay fruit set by choosing a bigger pot? And what is the best way to go about this? Do you gradually pot up to slightly larger pots as the plant grows or do you plant the seedling into the final pot size?    Could gradually potting up mitigate the fruit set delay? Of course I dont want to delay fruit set if I can help it.  And of course I dont want to pot up multiple times. I would be very grateful if you comment what works for you when growing peppers in pots? Thank you!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2022-02-01", "text": "\"But the bigger the pot size the longer the plant's roots will take to fill the soil volume. And then apply that same theory to planting in the ground. The ground soil volume is virtually endless and there is no way the pepper's roots would \"fill the soil\" so theoretically, it would never have significant shoot growth or fruit development. And we all know that's not true :-) There is no reason to assume the response would be any different in a container. Like Kate, I pot up my seedlings into the finished size container I choose. title: Pepper transplants:  bury stems or not? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "katyajini", "author_name": "katyajini", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/katyajini", "date": "2022-02-01", "text": "Without thinking too much about it I have been planting pepper plants in the ground more or less flush with where the soil level was previously.  With very young seedlings I dont worry about it too much and have buried the stem if the seedling becomes leggy.  I *think* the nascent tissues of young seedlngs are mutable and I have not faced problems. Now I hear from two staunch camps.  One, where it is advised not to bury the stems at all as it can lead to stunting and stem rot.   The other where the stem is buried one or more inches as a matter of course. Both these types of gardeners are growing peppers just fine.  So I guess it does not matter too much?  Or is there a 'better' way, for most part, to plant peppers  in the ground?  Should  one bury the stems or not? Thanks!", "images": []}

title: Replacing popcorn ceiling? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-84657643", "author_name": "HU-84657643", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-84657643", "date": "2022-02-01", "text": "Hi, I was up in my attic checking on something yesterday and stepped in an area where I wasn't supposed to step on and fell through...There is a huge hole in one of our bedrooms now. Since we will need to fix the hole in the ceiling, we were thinking of just replacing the whole ceiling since it is an old popcorn ceiling we've been wanting to replace. The issue though is that it is positive for asbestos (we had it tested about a year ago). I'm not too knowledgeable about ceiling stuff, and wanted to know...are we able to just replace the whole ceiling in that room, or do we have to scrape/remove the popcorn/asbestos first and then replace it? I am just looking for the safest and most efficient and economical route for this project. And who would be the best professional to contact for this job? Any advice would be greatly appreciated. Thank you!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~251783376", "author_name": "Beth H. :", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~251783376", "date": "2022-02-01", "text": "the safest would be not to disturb it and just cover it w/something else. Encapsulate w/special paint, and then cover the whole thing w/wood, beadboard, paneling, etc. Encapsulation means covering an asbestos material so it cannot release asbestos dust. Asbestos popcorn ceiling can be covered with new ceiling panels or vinyl paint. One way to cover popcorn ceiling is with gypsum board ceiling panels. This material is like drywall but lighter.         The problem w/disturbing it and scraping it is the dust: If you want to cordon off the other rooms, the air vent and wear proper gear, you might be able to do it yourself. Keep the popcorn ceiling wet to prevent dust from contaminating the air. Place asbestos-containing waste in sealed and properly-labeled plastic bags. Call a trash-pickup or landfill service that is equipped to accept asbestos in advance to make arrangements for removal/disposal. 2 videos on how to https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PO6cGcOb2DY https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=71xYVjoQ5pk It might be easier just to call in a company and get them all removed.   run a test on all ceilings and see what the percentage is.   was the home built before 1977? if you have someone come in and do the one room, you may as well get the other rooms done while they're there.  the cost is labor and ssetting up containment.  you don't want to pay for that twice!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/61a211df01f9bd45_6875-w240-h339-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/dd72226001f9bd45_6870-w240-h180-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/fd421ffe01f9bd46_6878-w240-h360-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/a2122b7b01f9bd46_6875-w240-h359-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

title: Save on Home Build | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "laith-khalilaljemzawi", "author_name": "Zelovian", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/laith-khalilaljemzawi", "date": "2022-02-02", "text": "Hello friends, We are looking to build our next home with a GC.  I have ideas on how best to save on this build, but would love some of your expert opinions!  For a bit more insight, I have some friends who are contractors, between them, myself, and some family, we plan to do some work on the house ourselves, and mostly want the GC to build the structure and finish out some critical areas for occupancy, leaving the rest for us. Money saving ideas so far: ---------------------------------------- - Limit corners / edges (square shape) - Keep the roof simple - Align bathrooms / plumbing - Leave most trim undone (DIY after build) - Finish some rooms only to drywall (Add ourselves after build) - Finish 1/2 of square only as attic (finish later as needed) - No built-ins outside of necessaries (We'll add later) - Standard door & window sizes - Building up (2 stories) Things we are trying to avoid sacrificing: ------------------------------------------------------------ - Overall size (Plan to grow into this house or build out for good resale value) - Kitchen, living room, master suite sizes. - Prominent morning room Any more ideas would be very much appreciated!", "images": []}

title: How to set up your HVAC to be able mitigate wildfire smoke? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "elaine-almeida29", "author_name": "Elaine Almeida", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/elaine-almeida29", "date": "2022-02-02", "text": "We are moving into a new house with an HRV integrated with the furnace and we want to be able to put in a better filter in the summer weeks with wildfire smoke. Do we need to upgrade the filters on the HRV or furnace or both? Implication I guess is that we would have to upsize the blowers on the systems we upgrade filters on?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "sktn77a", "author_name": "sktn77a", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/sktn77a", "date": "2022-02-02", "text": "Catch 22.  If you upgrade your blower, you will probably have to upgrade your ductwork!  I suspect that would be a non-starter...........", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "charles-ross-homes-pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "author_name": "Charles Ross Homes", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/design-build-firms/charles-ross-homes-pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "date": "2022-02-06", "text": "Hi, Elaine, If your home were an air-sealed box and fresh air was introduced only via the HRV you could design a system with a high-efficiency filter for the HRV to be used when wildfires occur.   But most homes don't behave like air-sealed boxes.  Instead, they operate at negative pressures due to the combination of wind, stack effect, and HVAC systems with undersized return air flows.  Air is drawn into the home though penetrations, cracks around windows and doors, etc.  For that reason, and given that wildfires are (hopefully) infrequent, I suggest you invest in air sealing your home to the extent practical, and balancing of your home's HVAC supply and return air flows.   When wildfires occur, turn off the HRV and use portable room air cleaners to filter ambient smoke inside your home.  You can move them from room to room as needed.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "terrasses-des-oliviers-paysagiste-paris-pfvwfr-pf~939909255", "author_name": "Terrasses des Oliviers - Paysagiste Paris", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/landscape-architects-and-landscape-designers/terrasses-des-oliviers-paysagiste-paris-pfvwfr-pf~939909255", "date": "2022-02-02", "text": "Bonjour \u00e0 tous, Situ\u00e9e \u00e0 Rueil-Malmaison, cette maison se trouve au fond d'une voie priv\u00e9e comptant 3 maisons au total. Les propri\u00e9taires ont fait appel \u00e0 nos services apr\u00e8s avoir rencontr\u00e9 plusieurs prestataires (piscinistes/paysagistes) qui ne trouvaient pas la solutions pour int\u00e9grer la piscine dans leur jardin, compte tenu de la configuration du lieu et des acc\u00e8s sp\u00e9cifiques (impossibilit\u00e9 de rentrer des machines type pelleteuse ou bobcat par exemple). Autre particularit\u00e9 \u00e0 prendre en compte : leur parking est situ\u00e9 sous le gazon, et la portance ne peut donc \u00eatre que de 250kg au m2. Pour r\u00e9pondre \u00e0 ces diverses probl\u00e9matiques, nous avons donc choisi de supprimer une partie des bambous qui servaient d'\u00e9cran v\u00e9g\u00e9tal et d'implanter la piscine sur la dalle en b\u00e9ton existante qui longeait le mur de la cl\u00f4ture et la maison. Le trou pour la piscine ainsi que l'\u00e9vacuation de la terre ont \u00e9t\u00e9 r\u00e9alis\u00e9s \u00e0 la main. La piscine fut pos\u00e9e en kit pour pouvoir l'acheminer dans le jardin ; un local technique a \u00e9t\u00e9 cr\u00e9\u00e9 derri\u00e8re les pots noirs dans le passage derri\u00e8re la maison. Pour cr\u00e9er une unit\u00e9 entre les espace piscine et d\u00eenatoire, nous avons rev\u00eatu le mur de bardage noir teinte charcoal, ponctu\u00e9 de luminaires. Nous avons enfin repens\u00e9 la v\u00e9g\u00e9tation dans l'ensemble du jardin afin de ne pas d\u00e9s\u00e9quilibrer celui-ci. Les drainages ont \u00e9galement \u00e9t\u00e9 revus par rapport \u00e0 la modification du terrain. La piscine est chauff\u00e9e par pompe \u00e0 chaleur. Nous avons choisi un ligner gris clair pour que l'eau ressorte verte. Elle est filtr\u00e9e par un filtre \u00e0 sable. Elle mesure 2.50 x 4 m\u00e8tres sur 1.60 de profondeur, il y a un escabanc \u00e0 l'int\u00e9rieur, servant \u00e0 la fois de banc et de marche pour sortir de l'eau. Le mobilier d'origine a \u00e9t\u00e9 conserv\u00e9. Le projet a co\u00fbt\u00e9 70 000 euros (piscine comprise), et le chantier a dur\u00e9 2 mois. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "homechef59", "author_name": "homechef59", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/homechef59", "date": "2023-09-06", "text": "I had a 6-burner Dacor gas cooktop with a separate downdraft unit. Like you, there was no possibility of using a hood.  I had to stick with the downdraft. Not optimal, but it was what it was. Here is what I learned in the process.  Both the Best and Zephyr downdrafts telescope up to 18\" making a larger area for drawing.  That's the biggest available.  They both come with a led light that lights up your cooking surface. title: Brick Siding Dampness Mystery | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "robyn-emsley", "author_name": "Robyn Emsley", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/robyn-emsley", "date": "2022-02-02", "text": "My house was built in 1980 and it is a raised bungalow ranch style with a poured concrete foundation that is 4 feet above grade. The rest of the home has brick and vinyl siding. There is one corner of the house on the North East side where the brick is always visibly damp where it meets the foundation. There is a new roof (2020), new gutters (2021) and no other plumbing in the area. We have been unable to determine what is causing this dampness. On the interior side of the dampness is a bedroom and the drywall is not moist according to a meter reading. The basement in that corner falls below the brick siding but there are condensation issues in the basement room there from incomplete fibreglass insulation. There are mortar cracks in the brick at this same corner which the previous owner partially repaired with some type of compound. There has been no wind-driven rain or snow that would have entered the brick cracks to cause this though. We've so far spoken to a structural engineer, two home inspectors, and the company that installed the gutters and have no answer/solution. Any thoughts?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/fe12e13301fab7a1_0967-w500-h604-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/4f52c50801fab7a2_0967-w500-h656-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: Induction Cooktops: Thermador Freedom Discontinued, now what? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jessica-ourisman", "author_name": "Jessica Ourisman", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jessica-ourisman", "date": "2022-02-03", "text": "TL;DR: Does wattage matter with induction cooking? A good sear is important and Miele has 7700W on their strongest burner vs. most others that max somewhere between 3500 and 5500. I had my heart set on the Thermador Freedom cooktop for my new kitchen. I ordered it back in October 2021 and paid in full at Ferguson. I thought all was well on its way with my construction completion date set for May 2022. I've just heard from Ferguson that Thermador has discontinued the Freedom. I've made calls to several other appliance stores and can't get a straigh answer other than it is impossible to order at this time and noone has one in stock. It has disappeared from the Thermador website, too. I am so sad, confused, and frustrated! So, I am back to the drawing board; trying to put the emotions aside and think rationally. I've been reading other reviews and discussions and most user manuals for other options. Thermador Liberty was the first contender for simplicity sake, but it seems overpriced when compared to competitors. What am I paying for if I can't have the Freedom's full cooking surface? Miele seems to be the stronger, more reliable, and more popular option. I prefer the look of F&P plus I've already ordered F&P fridge/freezer columns and the cooldrawer (ovens and diswasher will be Bosch). title: Paving Stone Sinking/Water Pooling | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-811368483", "author_name": "HU-811368483", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-811368483", "date": "2022-02-04", "text": "Obviously with the weather currently, it's been very cold. The past few days it's been 40 degrees and very rainy. There is water pooling outside of my back door on the paving stone, and after taking a couple steps I stepped on a stone that sunk about an inch or two into the ground, while the adjacent stones are loose as well. This is not a new walkway so I figure everything should be settled at this point. There is also a drain pipe from my house going into the ground about 4-5 feet away. Would it make sense that a drywell is under my walkway and that's what is causing the problems? And why would it happen now after 10+ years. I do not have the skills to replace this myself although if the job isn't complicated I am willing to try.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mindshift", "author_name": "mindshift", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mindshift", "date": "2022-02-17", "text": "It seems unlikely a drywell would have been placed so close to your home. But something is undermining your paving stones. Commercially built drywells are either concrete or high density plastic with a life expectancy of 30 years, but homemade drywells can be made of metal or plastic barrels surrounded by and sometimes filled with coarse stones to allow collected water to seep into surrounding soil. These may have a shorter lifespan. Do you have any plumbing lines that run under this paving? Even a small leak could cause the shifting of base materials. Do you have a high water table? Gravel and paving tends to sink into consistently wet ground. I would try to find out where outdoor supply and drainage lines run. Fixing the problem usually requires removing the paving stones that are settling, filling in more sand or gravel to support the stones, then replacing them. Start at the loosest stone, and use a spade to tip up one edge. Ideally you would have a level to raise up any subsidence, a tamper to pack down additional sand or gravel, and a rubber mallet to tap the pavers back into place. But you could use any straight stiff item like a pipe to eyeball low spots. You can use a wide flat board, even an old cutting board, laid over the fill and walked on. Use a short piece of wood placed between the paver and a regular hammer to protect the paver from chipping. It can be very difficult to find someone to make minor repairs; they generally want to completely replace the pavers. Here is an article with video on doing it yourself.", "images": []}}

title: Marigolds, Snapdragons and Aphids? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "debandmark123", "author_name": "debandmark123", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/debandmark123", "date": "2022-02-04", "text": "Hi Everyone, I hope this is ok to post here. I just bought half bloomed snapdragons yesterday from the store for the hummingbirds in the area. I live in a climate to where it's the optimal time to have them. These are potted and will be container plants outside on the porch. I previously had petunias in other pots and they bloomed fine but the aphids were a nightmare. Neem oil, while effective was really too harsh for them in the pots. I am hoping for a more natural alternative and so I was thinking maybe I can plant the marigolds in with the snapdragons due to them being an aphid repellent. Is that something that works well with the snapdragons and to keep most of the aphids at bay? I do want to still be able to attract the hummingbirds though. Will the marigolds deter them?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "purpleinopp", "author_name": "Tiffany, purpleinopp Z8b Opp, AL", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/purpleinopp", "date": "2022-02-07", "text": "If the petunias were blooming well, why worry about aphids?  One pot with a few plants is not much to rely on if one wants to attract any kind of wildlife.  If you have the discipline to change the sugar water daily, a hummingbird feeder is an ideal way to get a good look at hummers.  I have hundreds of various nectar-producing blooms in my yard on a given day during the warm part of the year but hummers go to the feeders much more often than any Lantana, milkweed, Salvia, or other single type of nectar plant.  I am not saying don't put nectar plants in your yard, but relying on a few snapdragons in a pot for the sole purpose of attracting hummers may not be as rewarding as you hope.  Having a few snapdragons in a pot because you love them and hope you might see a hummer visiting them is a great idea. National Audubon Society has published this warning about using neem oil outside on blooming plants: * A note on the use of neem oil, which is an insect growth inhibitor and non-toxic to birds. Because neem oil prevents insects from developing further, it can prevent bee larvae from developing if adult bees feed them neem oil-coated pollen they've brought back to the hive. title: Updating a 1960s recipe for Hungarian meatballs and sauce | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "originalpinkmountain", "author_name": "l pinkmountain", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/originalpinkmountain", "date": "2022-02-05", "text": "My Dad was complaining about the lack of variety and blandness in his diet (ironic because he is so picky which excludes most foods with any flavor or combinations of ingredients) but it is what it is.  One of the things he said he liked but couldn't make was meatballs.  Being mostly vegetarian and not liking the meats used for meatballs anyway, I do not have any experience making them.  But I hauled out one of Mom's community cookbooks from the early 60s which she and many of our family friends contributed to, hoping to find some ideas. One of our closest friends who died last year from covid, (after surviving the Holocaust with her mother in a work camp in her youth) was from Hungary and the cookbook contained one of her recipes that my Mom contributed.  Its for meatballs in a tomato sauce, which calls for ketchup and sour cream as the flavoring.  I'll make it more spicy with real Hungarian spices and use tomato paste to thicken the sauce, but the other ingredient that stumps me is \"a can of drained kidney beans.\"  So that takes the dish more into the realm of what I grew up knowing as \"goulash\" which was hamburger, noodles, tomato sauce and whatever else the particular cook wanted to throw in . . . So I'm not sure whether to just brown the hamburger without making meatballs, and then throw in the kidney beans and make the sauce and then serve over noodles, (which in this case would probably be macaroni), or make the sauce and then add the meatballs and kidney beans and serve over some type of longer noodle, which right now would have to be broken up fettuccine because of the egg noodle shortage.   That seems a little weirder to my experience, particularly because in that case I would want to throw some Parmesan cheese over the top, which isn't Hungarian.  I used to live in a town where I could get fabulous Bulgarian creamy feta, but not around here.  Even the regular feta is sub par.  I could also serve the meatballs with a shorter pasta, like bow ties or macaroni, I'm just not familiar with eating them that way.  Even when I eat them, or make vegetarian ones, they get served with long noodles of some sort . . . but I am open to expanding my culinary experiences, lol! Anyone ever had or made a Hungarian dish of similar ilk?  I want to stick as close as possible to the original recipe, which does not say what to serve it over.  I very often make dishes from recipes passed down from departed balabustas to honor their spirit.  \"Balabusta\" is Yiddish for \"boss\" in the sense of \"master home maker\" or \"master of the house.\" the \"a\" on the end means it's describing a woman, Balabos is the male version.  Nowdays it means something more akin to modern slang of \"boss\" as in \"that's a boss outfit\" or \"she's a real boss musician.\" etc. Ava's Meat Balls and Sauce 1.5 lbs ground beef 1 small onion minced paprika for color 1 tsp. A1 sauce 1 tsp. minced parsley 1/2 tsp. oregano 1/2 tsp. rosemary 1.5 tsp. salt 1/4 tsp. pepper Form 11-12 meatballs, roll in bread crumbs, brown in hot oil. Sauce 1 8oz. can of tomato sauce 3/4 tsp. salt 1/3 c. ketchup (I think I would use tomato paste here, with maybe a little garlc, paprika and red wine for seasoning) 1/2 cup sour cream 1 can kidney beans, drain and rinse Combine ingredients.  Add meat balls; simmer about 10 minutes.  Serves 4-6.", "images": []}

We\u2019ve had a long saga in trying to get a Frigidaire refrigerator that doesnt have problems.  we replaced a 10 year old Samsung that suddenly stopped working 3 years ago.  we purchased  a frigidaire professional model #FPBC2278UF from a local well known appliance store.  This is a freezer on the bottom, counter depth unit.    We  started having problems within a year - food freezing in refrigerator section, condensation around the freezer drawer seal and the freezer drawer was bent and would not close correctly.  Water would form large puddles in the floor.  Numerous service calls and replacement parts did not repair it.  Frigidaire replaced it but this took quite a long time due to pandemic shortages.  The second one had  exactly the same issues.  on the first service call for this one Frigidaire immediately authorised a replacement.  Again a long wait due to shortages.  the third one was delivered with numerous dents and scratches and also a bent drawer.  we refused it.  a fourth was delivered with a bent drawer, we refused it.  we received number five yesterday  it appears to be working but its a bit soon to say for certain.  While the door dents and dings were most likely related to rough handling in transport the freezer drawer issue appears to be a factory problem.  So buyer beware.  Thanks for reading and I hope this helps someone avoid the drama that we\u2018ve experienced.", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "3onthetree", "author_name": "3onthetree", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3onthetree", "date": "2022-02-08", "text": "@HU-840490612 nice catch, but I don't think the 3\" lintel bearing (4\" min, 6\" recommended) would cause all 3 different locations of cracks (maybe the one adjacent to it), because the lintel is bolted to the wood header. So this problem should be put back on the builder to rectify, but you should always be armed with as much information as possible when conflicts arise. So I am postulating about what may have caused this, which is only an assumption based on 2 pictures, but it could help direct someone in what to look for or engage you to stand your ground on the matter: - I would guess you'll find no stress cracks in the foundation stem wall, and no evidence of poor footings or settling. I say that because of the confined cracks in the middle of the door jamb and above the opening, and the stress cracks have routed through a couple bricks. - It looks like you have an attempt at a portal frame, where the LVL header extends to the outer wall. Sheathing is then closely fastened to create a very stiff 'L' leg, but I am guessing they didn't do this. - Consider that the header should not only be sized for the roof (and lateral) loads, but the weight of the masonry. There is not a lot of psf of brick above the opening, however, the LVL is designed, and allowed, to have a certain amount of deflection (a 16' span @ L/240 = 3/4\"). - The steel lintel is attached to this LVL. Even so, the lintel could be undersized. I would expect a L6x4x3/8\". - The bricks are then attached to the sheathing, most often by using the corrugated strap version of ties, where they will allow some movement, but not if they were angled high above the course joint. So picture the LVL naturally deflecting, it has a stiff enough connection at the ends, the ties didn't allow the brick differential movement, and you get stress cracks at these locations:   Things to look into then: - foundation - LVL size and deflection - portal frame or not - masonry ties (weeps and flashing while you're at it) - lintel size and fastening to LVL - whether repair of the mortar joints will crack again in the future from varying loads on the LVL changing it's deflection amount", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/85f226430202a750_1072-w240-h129-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

title: Tie down limbs to promote branching? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "travisaz", "author_name": "Travis in PHX (9b)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/travisaz", "date": "2022-02-06", "text": "Spring flush is right around the corner in Phoenix (in fact, it's already started for my grapefruit). My Meyer lemon lost many of it's leaves during the summer and early winter. Any new growth has been on the tips. So I have bare limbs with tufts of leaves on the tips. These tips are also growing fairly long. I want to reduce growth at the ends and encourage branching to fill out the bare middles. But I don't want to pinch off or trim the ends, because I will lose a substantial amount of remaining foliage and likely limit my flowering and fruit production for this season.As an alternative, I was thinking of tying these long branches down. My understanding is that will encourage growth at the new \"high\" point instead of the end of the branch.Has anyone done this? Is this a reasonable technique to try?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ef21f63c020015da_2766-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "bonsai-citrus_and_indoor_gardening", "author_name": "bonsai_citrus_and_indoor_gardening", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bonsai-citrus_and_indoor_gardening", "date": "2022-02-07", "text": "I've been doing this on my trees with pretty good results for several years now. In fact, I used the method to fix the canopy on my Nagami, which grew on only one side as, before I got it, someone removed all branches on one side of the tree. I also hesitated to trim that tree as it had very little foliage left when I got it.   Here's a recent one I did, the wire is the branch I pulled down, the one that isn't wired sprang up in the last two weeks.   Here's one I did a few years ago. It works fairly well, but there are a few things I've noticed. 1. You need to make sure that the tip of the branch is angled towards the ground or your branching will grow weird and it will produce growth from the tip of that branch. 2. You need to stay ahead of the new growth. This means that any time a branch gets big and long, wire it AS SOON as you can and while it is soft. You have a lot more leeway with the branch while it is soft and rubbery than when it hardens. Make sure to stay ahead of the new growth. 3. If you're doing this outside, use something that won't heat up, or fabric wrapped wire so that it doesn't heat up and damage the tree. Or paint it white. You can also use Jute to pull down the tips of branches, tied off the trunk. I did that in the early years with my Nagami before I got the wire. If done right you can really get some nice shape from a tree without removing a ton of branches and without significant pruning.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/6f622ee4020138f8_7293-w240-h180-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/1be20c25020138fa_7293-w240-h180-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

I left it laying on the soil to see what it would do. After about a year it rooted and started growing. When it got big enough, I noticed that many of the new leaves were lobed, like some types of desert cactus.   I showed it to my partner, and they said, \"That's not a Christmas cactus, silly! It from one of my regular cacti.\" I believed them, but I was puzzled because I've never seen a cactus in their collection with leaves shaped like these. Then I found another lobed leaf on a cutting while I was potting it after rooting it in water. This leaf was very hairy, like a cactus with spines.   I know this isn't a desert cactus. main_question: {"author_id": "lucillle", "author_name": "lucillle", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lucillle", "date": "2022-02-07", "text": "I have had a flatware set for many years and no longer have a bunch of the pieces.   I can either try to find replacements to my no longer made pattern which are available on Ebay, or buy a whole new set of some other brand/pattern.   My set was made in Japan and I've washed them in the dishwasher a zillion times, and never any rust.     I've looked at new sets on Amazon made by other companies, not cheap (but not the most expensive) and it surprised me to see in the reviews that some of the stainless pieces especially the knives rusted. Have you ever found rust on your stainless?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "outpaientzero", "author_name": "outpaientzero", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/outpaientzero", "date": "2022-02-07", "text": "Stainless flatware is made from different grades of stainless and some will rust easier than others.  Flatware referred to as 13/0  or 18/0 stainless will rust and lose it's shine and what these companies on amazon are peddling.  The first number is the amount of chromium and the last is nickel.  Good stainless flatware is 18/8 and 18/10 and what you should look for.  If the reviews said they rusted believe them and don't even consider the junk. I have two sets, and parts of a third and the cheapest with no shine left.  A magnet will stick strongly to a few spoons and less to others because the manufacturer didn't care what stainless they used and had no quality control. Un garage et une cave enterr\u00e9e. Notre famille s'est agrandie cet \u00e9t\u00e9 avec l'arriv\u00e9e de notre 2\u00e8me cacahou\u00e8te, notre bureau est devenue sa chambre. Le covid a aussi chang\u00e9 un peu nos boulots et nous t\u00e9l\u00e9travaillons plus. Dans ce contexte, nous envisageons de r\u00e9aliser une extension de notre maison pour agrandir notre salon (28 m\u00b2 avec la salle \u00e0 manger) et faire un espace bureau. Deux id\u00e9es, avec une m\u00eame base d'extension \u00e0 l'est de la maison, en ouvrant au niveau de l'actuel bureau : - faire un extension d\u2019environ 15 /20 m\u00b2 en RDC pour faire un lin\u00e9aire bureau c\u00f4t\u00e9 nord et le salon c\u00f4t\u00e9 sud. - faire une extension de 12 m\u00b2 sur deux niveaux, avec un escalier c\u00f4t\u00e9 nord (rangement dessous), salon au sud, et grand bureau \u00e0 l'\u00e9tage avec un convertible. Nos besoins : - salon plus grand, avec r\u00e9am\u00e9nagement complet si besoin - du rangement : on est semi minimaliste (ex : assez de v\u00eatements pour tenir 1 semaine mais pas plus, quantit\u00e9 de jouets limit\u00e9, on sort au max ce qui ne va plus rapidement ...), mais force est de constater qu'avec 2 enfants ayant 5 ans d'\u00e9carts, on va avoir 2 fois plus de jouets qu'avant. Le rangement peut \u00eatre dans l'extension (dessous escalier si \u00e9tage) ou dans la partie existante mais accessible facilement aux enfants. - lin\u00e9aire de bureau pour 2 personnes avec un \u00e9cran mini 20 pouces chacun et place pour le PC portable ouvert, clavier, souris. L'imprimante est aujourd'hui en wifi dans le placard de l'entr\u00e9e, si elle peut venir dans le bureau c'est bien mais pas indispensable (c'est une grosse laser). - cerise sur le g\u00e2teau : trouver une solution pour faire plus de rangement dans la chambre de notre grande qui fait tout juste 9m\u00b2 (chambre au sud mitoyenne au dressing). J'ai bien conscience que nos plans sont pourris, c'est la seule chose qu'on a r\u00e9ussi \u00e0 r\u00e9cup\u00e9rer \u00e0 l'achat. Je rajoute le plan du cadastre (le terrain fait 24m N/S x 21m E/O, il reste 10 m entre l'est de la maison et la limite du terrain) et quelques photos. Tous les plans sont bien avec le nord en haut. Ne pas h\u00e9siter \u00e0 me demander des \u00e9l\u00e9ments suppl\u00e9mentaires. Pour la partie copropri\u00e9t\u00e9, de nombreuses extensions ont d\u00e9j\u00e0 \u00e9t\u00e9 accept\u00e9es et r\u00e9alis\u00e9es. Le PLU indique 3m de la limite du terrain. On a d\u00e9j\u00e0 des id\u00e9es mais je ne veux pas orienter / brider vos solutions avec les miennes (qui sont d'ailleurs pas fameuses).       Merci d'avance \u00e0 tous pour vos super id\u00e9es. title: Hiding a minisplit in a cabinet vs. airflow requirements | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-91620898", "author_name": "David Huang", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-91620898", "date": "2022-02-08", "text": "My architectural plans call for installing a minisplit inside of a cabinet (with a slatted door for airflow), but my GC's HVAC sub told me this won't work as the units need 4 - 6 inches of space above the unit for airflow.  But, when I google \"minisplit hidden in cabinet\" I see lots of examples of them installed in what look like fairly tight spaces, i.e. definitely without 4-6 inches space above the units, and also with airflow partially obstructed by the slatted cabinet door as well. They look great...but are they functional?  How important is the manufacturer's recommended 4-6 inches in reality?  I find if I ask anyone from Mitsubishi or an HVAC installer they'll recommend against it but maybe that's just sticking to the script.  Perhaps this voids the manufacturer warranty, and/or the installer will do it but won't provide any warranty on it. We're installing a few of these and want to hide them all in cabinets...we've compromised to make the cabinets taller than originally planned for 2 out of 3 locations so that there's ample space for airflow, so problem solved for those. But there is one left where we'd really like to be able to fit it above a closet door (80\" high with the HVAC installed recessed into the space above the closet such that the slatted door is flush with the closet door) 96 inch ceiling and HVAC unit is 11.625 inch height, there would be a shelf at top of closet at 80\"...so if the unit doesn't need any clearance at the bottom, we'd have 4 inches of clearance at best, partially obstructed.  So seems borderline but if the 4-6 inches of room for airflow isn't in practice that important, perhaps we are just fine. Thanks!", "images": []}

title: Engineered wood: does wear layer matter besides ability to refinish? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "alex0c", "author_name": "alex0c", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/alex0c", "date": "2022-02-08", "text": "I understand that you need a 3mm+ wear layer (veneer thickness) if you want to be able to sand and refinish engineered hardwoods. My question is does the thickness of the veneer make a difference for anything else such as durability and scratch/chip resistance, or is that more a function of the protective coating on top and/or the core underneath? My builder only offers one engineered hardwood in the color we want and the veneer is only 1.2mm thick (overall plank thickness 3/8 inch). Frankly I'm not concerned about the ability to sand and refinish them because at that cost and mess level we'd probably be more inclined to just replace the floor. I am concerned though that the thinner veneer might be more susceptible to scratches and chips. Of course, the manufacturer hypes up the hyper durable coating claiming it's \"the most durable, impact-resistant hardwood on the market\". It's a Shaw Duras product with the Repel waterproof coating. I have seen terrible reviews for another Shaw line called Epic (their cheapest line) but this product is $1-2/sf more expense so not sure if it's any better.", "images": []}

For example, we found a Riobel shower system (rainforest head, regular shower head, controls) for $1100 and sink faucet for $280 at a kitchen & bath store. However, the same stuff, different brands (delta, American standard, casainc,etc.) at Lowe\u2019s are like $300-$400 shower and $100 sink. Is the difference in quality really worth it? If I buy the Lowes stuff am i going to be replacing it in a couple years? Why the huge price difference?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "blazedog37", "author_name": "Helen", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/blazedog37", "date": "2022-02-09", "text": "It really is brand specific. Delta and Moen are high quality brands. They actually have fixtures that are quite expensive as cost depends on the style and the finish. I am reasonably certain that a $100 faucet at Home Depot from Delta or Moen would be what is commonly referred to as \"builder grade\" - e.g. the least expensive style in the least expensive finish. There are of course cheaper brands that aren't good quality and typically bargain shoppers purchase these brands when they are looking for a certain style and/or finish at a bargain price. I would not consider getting anything less quality than a Delta or Moen for a shower or tub because you really don't want to deal with changing or repairing those as it is difficult and expensive to do in the future. Sink faucets are more easily changed as any reasonably competant DIY can do that. Price isn't a guarantee of quality but generally if you are looking for an upgraded style in an upgraded finish it is going to be more expensive comparing equivalent brands. Delta and Moen make upgraded styles and finishes and the price reflects that even though they might be less expensive than more upscale brands. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "3onthetree", "author_name": "3onthetree", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3onthetree", "date": "2022-02-15", "text": "@qam999 and @mcarroll16, notice I did not call out specific items good/bad or agree/disagree, just a general statement. It does feel that the OP is getting hammered by some of the same repeated comments that are stamped to suburban U.S. houses, which may not be warranted here, especially with so little information. Also not that either of you have here, but often so many commenters say their piece but they cannot even read drawings or understand why things are the way they are, and some of them even consider themselves \"Pro.\" So I will tell you what I saw that countered some comments, causing me to jump in originally: - I see a narrow lot of about 50', with a zero lot line on one side. Apparently an urban area, with some adjacent constraints. That can limit the shape of the footprint and opening up the side walls. - I see wet bathrooms, a common occurence in Europe and Asia. The little triangle represents a showerhead, so the Guest has a full bath, the Powder does not have a shower. - I see wardrobe cabinets, not built-in closets, a common occurence in Europe and Asia. - I see a kitchen that follows many utilitarian designs across the globe. Cabinets are furniture, and sometimes still travel with you. Some appliances are cabinet/appliance combos. Kitchens are not necessarily the central congregration area like in the U.S. Pantries are not huge as stocking up is not the norm. Laundries are not tasks to be celebrated, often there is a small combo condensing washer/dryer. Storage is not as critical as in the U.S., as other cultures just don't buy stuff, stuff, and more stuff to take care of their stuff. - I see a Living area that is not grouped to Dining and Kitchen. The U.S. way of living is to have large, open, communicating functions, not necessariy the norm in other parts of the world. - I see a small outside backhouse area and cafe table sized patio. Probably just for a burner to keep smells out of the house, hang laundry, and a table area that fits the lifestyle of just morning coffee. Many urban areas don't prioritize huge outdoor living/eating areas for huge parties. So, there are many things pointed out in the comments that can be improved with this plan, as I alluded to originally. But when commenting on a design, sometimes you have to shift gears to what, where, and why it is for that particular location, not just site, but country and culture. I\u2019d also like larger & more fenestrated leaves, but I\u2019m impatient & I understand that I have no choce but to wait for it to grow out of its juvenile phase.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2022-02-13", "text": "I wrote a piece comparing peat and pine bark to coir and coco husks a while back. You'll find some interesting facts and observations in it that should be helpful. Peat vs. Coir Sphagnum peat and coir have nearly identical water retention curves. They both retain about 90-95% of their volume in water at saturation and release it over approximately the same curve until they both lock water up so tightly it's unavailable for plant uptake at about 30-33% saturation. Coir actually has less loft than sphagnum peat, and therefore, less aeration. Because of this propensity, coir should be used in mixes at lower %s than peat. Because of the tendency to compact, in the greenhouse industry coir is primarily used in containers in sub-irrigation (bottom-watering) situations. Many sources produce coir that is high in soluble salts, so this can also be an issue. Using coir as the primary component of container media virtually eliminates lime or dolomitic lime as a possible Ca source because of coir's high pH (6+). Gypsum should be used as a Ca source, which eliminates coir's low S content. All coir products are very high in K, very low in Ca, and have a potentially high Mn content, which can interfere with the uptake of Fe. Several studies have also shown that the significant presence of  phenolic allelopathic chemicals in fresh coir can be very problematic for a high % of plants, causing poor growth and reduced yields. I haven't tested coir thoroughly, but I have done some testing of CHCs (coconut husk chips) with some loose controls in place. After very thoroughly leaching and rinsing the chips, I made a 5:1:1 soil of pine bark:peat:perlite (which I know to be very productive) and a 5:1:1 mix of CHCs:peat:perlite. I planted 6 cuttings of snapdragon and 6 cuttings of Coleus (each from the same plant to help reduce genetic influences) in containers (same size/shape) of the different soils. I added dolomitic lime to the bark soil and gypsum to the CHC soil. After the cuttings struck, I eliminated all but the three strongest in each of the 4 containers. I watered each container with a weak solution of MG 12-4-8 with STEM added at each watering, and watered on an 'as needed basis', not on a schedule. The only difference in the fertilizer regimen was the fact that I included a small amount of MgSO4 (Epsom salts) to provide MG (the dolomitic lime in the bark soil contained the MG, while the gypsum (CaSO4) in the CHC soil did not. In both cases, the cuttings grown in the CHC's exhibited < 1/2 the biomass at summers end as the plants in the bark mix. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "patricia-colwell-consulting-pfvwus-pf~1199761428", "author_name": "Patricia Colwell Consulting", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/interior-designers-and-decorators/patricia-colwell-consulting-pfvwus-pf~1199761428", "date": "2022-02-10", "text": "Look for an indepedant kitchen designer they generally have some good experience with bathroom design too do not go with a cabinet salesperson for sure.  IMO there is no way to successfully design a space remotely . I di a kitchen design in Miami Beach remotely but only after   being in the space and able to see it in person and also take every tiny meaurement on site.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "blazedog37", "author_name": "Helen", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/blazedog37", "date": "2022-02-10", "text": "Good luck finding someone. In my experience having someone who is local is critical for all kinds of reasons and especially so for kitchens and bathroons. A good designer wants to \"inhabit\" the actual space in order to get a true sense of the space and the light. I did a gut remodel and after everything had been moved out she came and just sat in the rooms for awhile. When picking finishes, the play of light and space is going to impact decisions - and that is part of the reason why you hire a professional in the first place. Also kitchens and bathrooms are particularly \"code\" specific and a good designer will be conversant with all of the necessary Codes and interface with the GC - a good GC will also obviously know Codes. However there are all kinds of issues which aren't necesarily Code but do impact functionality like where fixtures should be placed or even where knobs and pulls should be placed. How high and where exactly for the toilet paper holder. I am focusing on what seems to be relatively trivial matters but the sheer number of decisions that have to be made is overwhelming and I was very happy that certain decisions were being made by a professional. She would ask me about certain things of course that *mattered* but even when she asked me how I wanted something done I would generally ask her what the functionality would be for the different options and/or aesthetically what her recommendation would be. My designer was also indispensable as a defacto \"project manager\" as I don't have the background of knowledge to truly judge construction. So she would either find things that needed to be corrected or would explain to me why things weren't an issue. Also a local designer will have resources in terms of all kinds of stuff - for my project there were the  \"to the trade\" sources so that we did a few visits to the Pacific Design Center. She also had artisans - cabinet makers; wall paper hangers; upholsters; custom furniture builders; regular \"to the trade\" vendors - and even with her designer markup the net price to me was generally lower than what I would have spent - and the expertise was *priceless*. I think remote can work if one is just looking for help in terms of furniture placement or whatever but I think for the kind of remodel of kitchens and bathrooms which OP is planning you really need a talented and experience designer who can be onsite.", "images": []}}

title: How to find and use realistic Inspiration photos given your "givens" | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "housegal200", "author_name": "housegal200", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/housegal200", "date": "2022-02-10", "text": "Are you planning a full renovation? Need to refresh one room? Or trying to choose the right wall or exterior paint for an existing house you're buying? New flooring? Here's the thing. Unless you're doing a new build, your present or future built home inside and out comes with a set of \"givens.\" \"Givens\" are the basic infrustructure of a building's exterior or interiors--the basic architecture, the materials, the built-ins, the flooring, etc. If you can't or won't change a given, say the kitchen cabinets or the flooring, or just have to have all gray or all black, then choose Inspiration photos with those same givens. A Design Dilemma Poster today is unhappy with her kitchen even though new cabinets and flooring are exactly what she chose--all gray floors, walls, cabinets. Several pros posted gorgeous photos of similar gray cabinets but with warm wood floors, white walls, and warm wood accent shelves. Sometimes people buy a Tudor house--the \"given\"--and want it to look \"farmhouse\" or \"midcentury.\" There are some changes that can be made with color, landscaping, and paint to give an updated look. But without a huge budget for structural renovations, the basic bones are Tudor. Instead of trying to turn it fully into what it's not, the buyer, before buying, should do a search on the major home renovation sites to see what updates are realistic and appealing given the budget. So how do you find the right Inspiration photos? Say you want new \"dark gray cabinets\" in your total kitchen renovation? Put that into the search engine box whether on Houzz, Google, or Pinterest. Pick the photos you like. Then carefully study the other materials and finishes in the photos you find. What color are the floors, the hardware, the appliances, the furnishings? What color are the walls? That's your palette for gray cabinets, and it's likely not going to be all gray everything. A pro would likely tell you that ahead of time. Instead the pros on the DD in question had to make suggestions given the \"givens\" the OP chose to install. Without getting too much into it, sometimes the \"given\" is a new sofa that doesn't fit or is all leather black. Or an OP can't/won't part with a family heirloom dining set. Many an OP has asked how to decorate a room and make it cozy with a massive black leather puffed out sofa (usually facing a massive black TV). Sometimes the OP says they want to take down a wall to accommodate the \"given.\" And often the Commentors suggest a change in layout and TV orientation will make the \"given\" less overwhelming. And someone like me will suggest that getting a new sofa or smaller TV will be cheaper than taking down a wall.", "images": []}

The tree I want to protect is on the left which inhibits dirt removal to an extent. main_question: {"author_id": "jessica-uhler65", "author_name": "Jessica Uhler", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jessica-uhler65", "date": "2022-02-11", "text": "We are about to start our kitchen remodel after planning it for about a year. Below is our mood board. -Cabinets are IKEA boxes (which I have REALLY gone back and forth on and second guessed, but when we started this project that was what our budget allowed) with custom painted wood shaker fronts from Niue Cabinets. -Perimeter counters are black soapstone - island is statuario marble with a gorgeous Rohl unlaquered brass bridge faucet. 2 Devol ceramic pendant lights over island unlacquered brass cabinet hardware - backsplash on range wall will be the same marble as the island at 15 or 18\" with a 4\" shelf. No uppers on that wall. - There will be a built in hutch on the other side of the island that will be our coffee bar area. Still trying to decide on the finish for that. - The floors are going to be refinished original fir The overall look we are going for is a timeless, British kitchen that looks like it's always  been here. The size of the project feels a bit overwhelming for me- it's 120 year-old house and we have a lot of renovations to do. It feels daunting to undertake one piece of it without having a cohesive vision for the entire thing. Attached or adjacent to the kitchen are a mudroom, dining room and powder room that all also need to be renovated. A million more decisions! The mistakes I'm trying to mitigate: Our ceilings are 113\" tall. I ordered 30\" cabinets with 15\" stacked on top, but that leaves me with a 12\" gap. I'd like to finish the cabinets all the way to the ceiling so they look custom and finished. Would it be possible to do transitional trim and cove moulding to get me to the ceiling or is that too big of a gap? The other option is I take back the 30\" IKEA boxes and get 40\" and then I have to reorder the custom fronts for those cabinets and eat the cost (around $1300- which is not fun but as a percentage of the overall project not a terrible mistake). If I go with the 40\" with 15\" on top, that leaves me with only 4\" and I'm not sure that's enough for a nice cove moulding. I'm a bit stuck here. Our IKEA sink cabinet is 36\"- but the sink I ordered is 33\".  From what I've read It seems that this is the correct size cabinet. I'm still not exactly clear how we need to modify the IKEA base cabinet but I have watched some tutorials on building a support for the sink. A big outstanding question is lighting: We will have the two ceramic DeVOl pendants over the island, undercabinet lighting, but I'm trying to figure out how light the rest of the room- I don't love recessed lights but they are very practical. I am trying to figure out if I can install a few (4?) small flush mount lights instead. Something like this orthis. But where exactly do I place them so they don't look random and still serve as task lighting to a certain degree? Centered in the path? Closer to the edge of the counters? I think I will do 2 small cans right over the sink. Would it be a mistake to not have can lighting in a kitchen with such high ceilings? I've seen it done before  (Jean Stoffer used the Rejuvenation bare bulb flush mounts in a project and it looks good, but i wonder if it lights the counters). Also trying to choose the light that goes over the kitchen table- something simple? . Or can it be more of a statement piece since the island lights are so simple? Another question is the backsplash- RIght now I have planned to do either a 15 or 18\" hight marble slab with a ledge shelf on the range wall (no uppers). We are planning to do a plaster hood with 2 sconces on either side (still need to choose the exact sconces). But I also love the rustic look of zellige tile. Wondering if it costs a fortune to install. The hutch we ordered (ours will be all wood and have raised panel doors instead of the farmhouse looking ones): We will be putting a marble counter on it and installing a small round bar sink. Debating between a deck mount bar faucet and a wall mount.  I will make another post about the mudroom and powder room- trying to tackle one project at a time... sort of. main_question: {"author_id": "3katz4me", "author_name": "3katz4me", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3katz4me", "date": "2022-02-11", "text": "Someone here may remember me asking last year if anyone had a Tesla and if so what their experience was with it.  Some kind person, whose name I don't recall, responded with very helpful info. So after much research and deliberation we ordered one in April 2021 and got it on 12/31/21.  This was entirely DH's idea - for some reason he really had it in his head that he wanted an EV/Tesla.  I on the other hand, having worked in an IT role most of my career, thought no way in h3!! do I want such a heavily computerized car.  I also thought DH, who is annoyed by updates/changes on his phone, would go nuts with a car that runs updates overnight and looks/functions different in the morning. Well fast forward and, after one month, we have settled in quite nicely with it.  It's his car and I've only driven it once but it was nice to drive.  He hasn't really had any trouble adjusting to it though there is a lot to learn.  I'm sure we only know a fraction of all that and we haven't taken it on any big trip yet so that will be an experience when the time comes - supercharging and all that. What's remarkable but not surprising is how much we save on fuel; i.e. off peak electric charging vs. gas.  We just got our electricity bill for January and the total for the car was $34 for the whole month.  I contrast that with filling up my car today at $60.  DH filled his up about once a week for about that amount - more often when driving to the lake in the summer.  The other astonishing thing, probably true with many new car purchases, is that the price to buy one now is 25% more.  So we could sell it for more than we paid for it but of course we aren't going to do that. The older I get the more I gravitate toward what is known and comfortable but I do think it's good to push yourself outside the comfort zone and try new things.  Every time I do I'm glad I did. In this case it was DH who did the pushing.", "images": []}

Green flower buds that have not opened yet may still open when environmental conditions are favorable again. My plants have delayed opening more blooms anywhere from several weeks later to slightly more than two months. Flower buds that turn brown were killed and may either quickly fall down or not. title: Spider Mites on Italian Cypress.... | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "david-ortins", "author_name": "David Ortins", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/david-ortins", "date": "2022-02-11", "text": "I have a row of 5 very tall, mature Italian Cypress in front of our house. When we bought it 6 years ago I noticed they had a lot of brown spots and didn't look very happy. I went to our local \"Master Gardener\" who said they were being overwatered and to cap the irrigation heads near them. I did that, and they haven't improved at all. A neighbor mentioned their lawn service told her our trees have spider mites, so I checked for them, and that seems to be the problem. I called an arborist that said he'd have to use a citrus ladder to reach the top of the trees and spray them all with miticide, two applications a week apart, and inject the soil around them with a fertilizer/ systemic miticide to prevent future infestations. He quoted about $2000 to do this. I could have the trees removed and new ones put in for about that price. The arborist called back today and said he did some research on-line and said we should wait until the summer when the mites are active. This is Florida, the ones that shook out onto a piece of paper were very active! I'm curious if anyone has had any luck treating spider mites on trees this big?", "images": []}

title: How Long for Bare Copper for Concrete-Encased Electrode UFERS? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-528228756", "author_name": "HU-528228756", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-528228756", "date": "2022-02-11", "text": "Difference of opinion here... Forms are up, wire is in and getting close to having pour done... Contractor has about 3 ft of copper going thru footer and clamped to 20+ ft of rebar (that in turn is tied to rebar all over... ) Our construction inspector (he's not an electrician) called that out saying 20 ft of copper is 'recommended'. Contractor countered that the copper going in connects to the rebar and makes a continuous ground. That does make sense to me. Reading a quote from NFPA \"There are two different methods for establishing this electrode. This electrode can be either a minimum of a #4 AWG bare copper conductor or it can be unencapsulated reinforcing steel rods with a minimum diameter of \u00bd inch. When this electrode consists of reinforcing steel, it is allowed to join multiple shorter sections of rods together through the usual methods but the final assembled length must meet or exceed 20 feet.\" You can narrowly slice and dice it as \"either\" \"or\" and \"must be 20 feet\" but there's some room for interpretation and I'm not sure I can really fault the way it is currently done.", "images": []}

title: Rhododendron That Does Not Bloom | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "westes", "author_name": "westes Zone 9b California SF Bay", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/westes", "date": "2022-02-12", "text": "I have two Horizon Monarch Rhododendrons in separate containers. The container soil is half small bark and half turface. The plants have survived for years in that soil. One of the two plants develops flower buds but never blooms. It looks to me like the plant has just enough energy to develop the first stage of the buds, but it lacks the energy to finish the process and actually bloom. The other plant blooms well. My questions: I realize these plants should be in the ground, but our soil will never support Rhododendrons.  I have been using Osmocote once a year, and people here assure me that Rhododendrons are not heavy feeders.  Other growers have told me to use Rock Phosphate with Boron (brand Espoma), although I do not understand if boron is a separate ingredient or is always included.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/1b72b0fe02101c56_3079-w500-h281-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/3672827502101c57_3080-w500-h281-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2022-02-18", "text": "It could very well be lack of water. Rhodies need plenty of water in late summer to fall when they set flower buds for the coming year. Lack of water at that time will result in flower buds not fully developing or aborting. Since the OP lives where there are few if any serious freezes, that is not the issue. Neither is excessive acidity - almost impossible to generate in a potted media and rhodies prefer and will tolerate a high level of acidity anyway. btw, fall blooming can be very common here and it does NOT affect the normal flowering cycle to any significant degree. Also not sure of the qualifications of the growers that suggested rock phosphate and boron but I would ignore them.  Per the American Rhododendron Society: \"The popular perception that rhododendron and azalea flowering is enhanced by phosphorus is incorrect.\" For containerized rhodies, an all purpose fertilizer, preferably one formulated for acid loving plants, once or twice a season is sufficient. They require very little. For rhodies planted in the ground, if the soil pH is sufficiently acidic, you may never need to fertilize these plants! There are massive 50+ y.o. rhodies in my garden that I doubt have ever been fertilized. They bloom heavily and like clockwork.", "images": []}}
