title: Greetings to all; rose news | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2022-02-12", "text": "First, hello to bart bart, and I hope you're doing well, and your garden.  It was good to see your greeting on the thread on compact roses. I haven't been posting much for a while, partly because Houzz irritates me, partly because I haven't done much with roses in late years beyond maintenance.  Some of this was pandemic-induced torpor; then, we had a very unpleasant summer in 2021 and I avoided the sun-blasted garden for months, choosing instead to clear brush down in the woods.  But this fall I got some energy back with the first rains, and ordered fourteen roses from Tuincentrum Lottum in the Netherlands, my first rose order in four years.  The order was divided between once-blooming old roses and Wichuriana ramblers, both classes that tend to do well here.  DH dug the holes; I amended them with masses of old hay and sand, the latter a novelty.  Organic amendment alone was still leaving the ground too heavy for certain kinds of roses I want to grow, warm climate roses and Hybrid Musks, so I thought I would try adding sand as well. In addition to the purchased roses, I filled holes in the rose beds with plants grown from suckers or cuttings, or rescued from locations where they were doing poorly:  HMs 'Francesca' and 'Kathleen', 'Mme. Zoetmans', 'Alfred de Dalmas'/'Mousseline' (I'm not sure which it is), a puny 'Austrian Copper', a red HP-looking rose, something I hope is 'Centifolia Alba', a 'Princesse de Naussau' that lost most of its roots getting dug up and which I hope will survive.  May should be exciting. We've had an unusually sunny dry winter, which has been bad for groundwater levels, but good for working outside.  I cleaned up two major rose beds, noting from the higher quality of the weeds that the ground is slowly improving, and have spent pleasant hours shearing, pruning, mulching, filling planting holes.  The garden is green in winter:  the grass is bright as emeralds, the Italian cypresses stand up straight and dark, the olives are silvery, and all the other plants, eleagnus, rosemary, Leyland cypresses, add their color and textures.  On a sunny day it's beautiful, in its untidy way. In addition to the roses, we filled in parts of hedges, planting photinia, forsythia, honeysuckle (L. etrusca), kerria, and perhaps some other odds and ends; and I began planting a low hedge in front of the rose beds, using rosemary, Mexican sage, phlomis, and shrub germander.  I want to continue the low hedge in front of both rose beds, but it will probably require a hundred plants at least, and digging to match, so is a major task. Rain is forecast for Valentine's Day, and I certainly hope it comes, because we need water.  Temperatures have been cool enough, but with the unusual amount of sun some roses have continued in bloom through the winter:  'Sanguinea' in particular, and, more recently, 'Comtesse du Cayla', 'Archiduc Joseph', and various other Teas.  Spring is coming soon, but the early flowers are a few weeks ahead of their usual schedule:  sweet violets, hellebores, early crocuses, miniature irises.  The winter aconite and snowdrops are in correct seasonal flower. Happy spring to all!", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2022-02-19", "text": "It's oedema, a physiological disorder. Something I wrote about it: Oedema (aka edema) is a physiological disorder that can affect all terrestrial plants. It occurs when the plant takes up more water than it can rid itself of via the process of transpiration. The word itself means 'swelling', which is usually the first symptom, and comes in the form of pale blisters or water-filled bumps on foliage. Under a variety of circumstances/cultural conditions, a plant's internal water pressure (turgidity) can become so high that some leaf cells rupture and leak their contents into inter-cellular spaces in leaf tissue, creating wet or weepy areas. Symptoms vary by plant, but as the malady progresses, areas of the leaf turn yellow, brown, brown with reddish overtones or even black, with older damage appearing as corky/ scaly/ ridged patches, or wart/gall-like bumpy growth. Symptoms are seen more frequently in plants that are fleshy, are usually more pronounced on the underside of leaves, and older/lower leaves are more likely to be affected than younger/upper leaves. Oedema is most common in houseplants during the winter/early spring months, is driven primarily by excessive water retention in the soil, and can be intensified via several additional cultural influences. Cool temperatures, high humidity levels, low light conditions, or partial defoliation can individually or collectively act to intensify the problem, as can anything else that slows transpiration. Nutritional deficiencies of Ca and Mg are also known contributors to the malady. Some things that can help you prevent oedema: * Increase light levels and temperature * Monitor water needs carefully \u2013 avoid over-watering. I'd heartily recommend a soil with drainage so sharp (fast) that when you to water to beyond the saturation point you needn't worry about prolonged periods of soil saturation wrecking root health/function. Your soil choice should be a key that unlocks the solutions to many potential problems. * Avoid misting or getting water on foliage. It slows transpiration and increases turgidity. * Water as soon as you get up in the AM. When stomata close in preparation for the dark cycle, turgidity builds. If you water early in the day, it gives the plant an opportunity to remove (for its own needs) some of the excess water in the soil. * Put a fan in the room or otherwise increase air flow/circulation. Avoid over-crowding your plants. Al", "images": []}}

There are 2 good ways to approach pruning off dead stubs of trees in containers. First is to cut flush to the trunk. This can be accomplished with a pruning saw, or, there are specialized tools made specifically for pruning flush. These tools, a concave cutter (top) or knob cutter (below) will remove branches and leave a concave depression in the trunk or lower order branch. When callus forms at wound edges and start to cover the wound, it will be least noticeable if a concave cutter was used.    The other method is to allow the short stub to stat on the plant for a year or so. The stub should have any green growth that occurs on it rubbed off, or the stub won't die back to the base. As the rest of the tree continues to grow, you'll see evidence of a branch collar forming around the base of the stub. The advantage of leaving the stub until a branch collar forms then cutting flush to the collar lies in the fact it allows the tree to completely compartmentalize the wound to keep any pathogens from spreading to living wood adjacent to the wound. For more on \"compartmentalization of decay in trees\" and how trees 'wall off' injuries, use the search words CODIT Shigo, or see Wikipedia for CODIT. Wounds heal faster if you can keep the tissue surrounding the wound moist. When the tissue surrounding the wound dries out, it increases the size of the wound, and callus will need to arise from the wound edges and roll over all the dead parts before the wound closes. I often cover all but small wounds with waterproof wood glue immediately. I 'paint' the wound, being careful not to get glue on the living bark surrounding the wound. Some use Vaseline or even Preperation H to cover wounds so they stay moist. They also make cut paste to cover wound of trees destined to live their lives in pots.  In the center is a large wound on a maple tree due to a trunk chop aimed at increasing a future bonsai tree's taper. title: Over / undermount sink for quartz counter | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-95346366", "author_name": "ACAC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-95346366", "date": "2022-02-14", "text": "First post here, so forgive me if I'm doing this wrong. We are doing a small midcentury modern kitchen: walnut cabinets, white quartz counters.  We've never had stone counters before, and are wondering: how common is it to get chips around the sink from washing dishes? Are we safer to get an overmount to avoid them? Background: we use the heck out of our kitchen.  Every summer we can a ton of food (last summer we did ~300lbs of tomatoes, 24 quarts of pickles, 24 quarts of peaches, etc etc), we make bread twice a week, cook almost everything from scratch, etc. We have two young kids and they're also in the kitchen with us.  This kitchen will work *hard* - including washing cast iron pans, canning pots, Le Creuset dutch ovens, etc -  so functionality is key. TL;DR: We love the 'crumb wiping' promise of undermount, but can't help but wonder if we're doomed to a chewed up sink rim without an overmount sink.  Thoughts?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~848525206", "author_name": "Joseph Corlett, LLC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~848525206", "date": "2022-02-14", "text": "\"How common is it to get chips around the sink from washing dishes?\" This has everything to do with sink edge profile selection and little to do with material or mount style. The larger and more round the edge at the sink, the less likely chipping will occur. All our sink replacement jobs get a 3/8\" radius. Show me a pencil edge at a sink and I'll show you a chip factory no matter the material. \"Are we safer to get an overmount to avoid them?\" This is a poor reason to get a top mount sink. You want a slight positive sink reveal. Negative reveals are crud hiders and expose the bottom edge of the stone to potential chipping. A flush reveal creates an elongated silicone joint line that frays and becomes ugly and unsanitary. A slight positive reveal protects the stone bottom and makes a tight maintainance-free joint between the stone borrom and the sink flange that never turns black/brown from leaking when strapped in place. You may want to consider a TopZero sink:", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/cf82b528020aa15d_3840-w240-h180-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/be1295e9020aa15f_3843-w240-h180-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

I do hand pollinate them when I notice they have a lot of flowers, and know for a fact that the last batch of fruits were hand pollinated several times. This year I've cut open 14 fruits so far, and not one has had a seed. I think this may be the result of no natural pollinators and the fact that I am pollinating the flowers myself (so I might not get to them at the exactly right time of day), but I'm curious if anyone else has noticed the same or if anyone has any ideas?", "images": []}

title: Experiences with triple pane windows in Northern Climate? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-254096870", "author_name": "Julia Thompson", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-254096870", "date": "2022-02-14", "text": "Hi all, My husband and I will be building a new construction in the norhern climate. We want the house to be energy efficienct but need to be cognisant of cost as well. We do plan on staying in the home for many years. What have other's experiences been using triple pane windows in regards to cost/return on investment? And, have others noticed a significant difference with how much light gets in/how bright the room feels compared to dual pane? Thanks!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "oberon476", "author_name": "oberon476", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/oberon476", "date": "2022-02-15", "text": "If asked I would always recommend triples for someone who is in climate zone 6 or higher. Whether dual or triple pane making sure that it's a good window with a good glass package that is installed correctly is much more important than the number of lites. I live in northwestern Wisconsin (a few miles from Minnesota border) where 17-19F is considered to be a reasonably comfortable high temperature for several months of the year. I do have triples and I wouldn't consider changing that if I were considering ever building again. For someone in climate zone 5 triples are likely to offer a bit of a comfort upgrade over duals but probably not much in the way of significant ROI if that is a priority. Whether triples are darker than duals depends mostly on the coating(s) used and to a lesser extent on the width of sash/frame since sash/frame is included in VLT calculations for the entire window package. A dual pane glass-only package using Cardinal's LoE-240 (picking on Cardinal since something like 65-70% of all residential coatings come from them), has a visible light transmittance of 40% whereas a triple with two separate LoE-180 coated lites will have a VLT of 70%. Even using LoE-366 with LoE-180 in a triple pane IGU make-up results in glass-only VLT of 57%, 17 percentage points higher than the dual pane. Examples are all for glass-only IGU configuration using 1/8\" lites. Thicker glass will result in lower VLT numbers, roughly 3 percentage points lower when using 1/4\" glass in place of 1/8\" for example.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "the3browns", "author_name": "the3browns", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/the3browns", "date": "2022-02-15", "text": "https://www.flickr.com/photos/195013108@N02/sets/72177720296693717 My fiance and I  recently bought a house and what we thought would be minor kitchen upgrades has somehow spiraled into a complete renovation. My biggest issue initially was the soffits that made the ceiling feel very low and the popcorn. My fiance's biggest issue was that the washer and dryer were in the kitchen, in a closet that shared a wall with the formal dining room and the living room. He hated the noise and I hated that he threw dirty clothes in the middle of the kitchen floor \"to be washed\". So, we had the soffits and popcorn taken out, and opened up the laundry closet as much as possible. We could not remove the wall dividing the laundry closet from the refrigerator space because the A/C drain pipe runs down that wall. We considered removing the pantry that opens into the informal dining/ breakfast area to open the kitchen up more, but that turned out to be load bearing. After using the kitchen for a while, I started to dislike the brick wall the housed the oven. It made it awkward to use the counter space right of the cooktop. Also, if I cooked at the stovetop with the oven on I would be blasted with heat from the front and back which was not fun. So we took that brick structure out and plan to replace it with a slide in range to save space (and $). Now it was obvious we would have to replace all of the cabinets and counter tops instead of painting and trying to find some that matched good enough to put the kitchen back together. There was an electrical panel in the laundry closet above the washer. I considered leaving it there and using the space under it for a trash/recycling cans or dog food bowls, or something, anything to save money but we couldn't figure out a solution that satisfied both me and the electrical code requirements. So, we bought a new panel and had it flipped to the opposite side of the wall, into the formal dining room where it will later be covered with some type of wall art. Now, we are trying to decide on the kitchen cabinet layout. The major issue is the location of the new range. The old cooktop and oven each had gas hookups, so I can place the range on either wall. Aesthetically, I prefer the range in the corner but I've never had one so there may be some disadvantages that I'm not seeing. I do worry about the amount of space the corner range eats up in a kitchen that already seems small in proportion to the house's other rooms. The upper cabinets also look weird to me with the range in the corner and an exhaust hood. I've always wanted an exhaust hood that wasn't mounted under cabinets, but it might look better with them. What do yall think? Please help save my kitchen! I would love any and all feedback, suggestions, etc. on how I can improve this layout. I am open to something entirely different as well, the only thing I cant move is the sink. (Kitchen is on a slab) I know the layouts aren't perfect- they are just visual aids for me and will be redone by our cabinet supplier at some point. Many thanks in advance!! title: Need Help Figuring Out Shower Leak & Steps to Repair | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "rielle-montague", "author_name": "riellebee", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rielle-montague", "date": "2022-02-15", "text": "While the shower in the bathroom above the kitchen was in use, water started leaking through a recessed light and a speaker opening in the ceiling.  The leak eventually stopped once we turned off the shower.  We think it might be an issue with the valve, but haven't done trouble-shooting yet.  (Our house was new construction when we bought it 2.5 years ago and no longer under warranty.)  I'd like to hire a plumber to fix this.  Because the shower fixtures are in/on a wall between a shower and bathtub alcove in the bathroom, the wall with the plumbing is tiled on both sides.  Is it possible to determine the source of the leak without removing the tile?  I called a couple of plumbers who said that they don't remove tile to address plumbing issues.  Another plumber offered to send a team of two plumbers to investigate through the opening once the trim is removed from the shower fixtures or through the hole in the ceiling below (avoiding tile removal).  I'm trying to figure out how to best get this resolved and whether I'll need a contractor and a plumber due to the tile.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/8bc2907d020bceec_1054-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/43f28407020bceee_1056-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/92828d9f020bcef1_1061-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1419066837", "author_name": "BobH", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1419066837", "date": "2022-02-15", "text": "Since you have a handheld sprayer, I would start by running the water through the handheld and fill up a couple buckets. Don\u2019t let the water get anywhere on the floor or walls of the shower. If the water leaks downstairs then you know the valve is leaking behind the tile. If there is no leak then spray water directly into the drain for a couple minutes. If no leak then spray it into one corner of the shower base for a minute. Check for leaks. Try this experiment, take out your shelves mark the back 20% with a piece of electrical tape.  Next get a magnetic whiteboard and marker for the front of your fridge. title: Contractor bids all over the place? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "njlibrarian", "author_name": "njlibrarian", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/njlibrarian", "date": "2022-02-15", "text": "I have been saving up for some time hoping to put a small addition on my 1950s Cape.  My hope was to add on a 165 SF space as a small family room--Basic oak floors, maybe 3 or 4 double-hung windows with trim on the front side, a glass door and simple stairs to the backyard, some electrical outlets, and a ceiling fan.  It would entail opening up an end wall (just behind the carrying beam that runs end to end down the house).  The opening with a new support beam would extend from behind the carrying beam to the back wall, and the add-on would go straight out to the side.  I didn't know if I would need to add some kind of minisplit, or could tie into my existing HVAC, so I figured that might also need to be added on to my budget.  (In my fantasy version, I would put in a gas fireplace, but I figured I could do that later.)  Not knowing much about construction costs, I tried to look into pricing to get a sense of how much I would need to have in the bank.  I kept seeing a very standard $80-$208 price PSF quoted on many informational Web sites.  Since I live in central NJ pretty close to Princeton, I used the top end as the base for my estimate, and figured I would need to add in additional for the floors, the windows, and door, plus for the foundation and other issues or adjustments that might arise.  Contractor #1 was recommended by 4 close neighbors, all of whom have used him for renovation projects (some multiple projects over time).  They all sung his praises, saying he was excellent, fair, did great work, kept close to his estimate except for unavoidable problems or their own changes.  He gave me an estimate coming to about $185 PSF (which I assumed would end up a bit higher in the end, but sounded reasonable as the starting amount), and said he could start in about 3 months, which I said was fine.  After that I never heard from him again.  Eventually, I tried to reach out to firm things up about any details, permits, etc. I might need to be on top of, but I got no reply to my texts (texted him 3 times over 8 weeks, with the last one about a month ago now).  Contractor #2 kept trying to sell me on adding a full kitchen remodel and doubling the square footage of the add-on.  In the end, he said he would \"write it up both ways,\" and then I never heard from him again.  Contractor #3 I had heard very good things about, but no one close to me had ever used. After asking me a lot of detailed questions about what I was hoping to do (and also inquiring about remodeling the kitchen at the same time, but not pushing it when I said I couldn't afford to add that on to this project), he said it would cost about $120,000--nearly $730 PSF.  I initially thought he meant including the kitchen (reader, he did NOT).  He was very nice, not condescending at all when I said that was above my budget.  I didn't say, Your bid is TOO HIGH.  I just said unfortunately, that sounded like more than I could afford or should realistically invest in this house in this neighborhood.  He asked what my other bids had been and I told him the details above.  He said that it was unlikely that anyone could do the job at the price Contractor #1 said ($185 PSF) \"without cutting a lot of corners.\"  Despite the slight snarkiness there, he actually was very nice.  But it left me wanting to say, I said 11x15, not 11x50.  Can such a modest addition with essentially nothing fancy to it (yes, I realize wood floors and decent windows and doors can add up, but can they add up to the tune of $120,000?).  I'm not sure where to turn now.  These two estimates are miles apart, and I have found it is nearly impossible to get anyone to even return a call.  If my idea that I can find someone who is skilled for $210 PSF+ is highly flawed, can someone let me know what might be a reasonable amount to expect to pay?  I'm not a person who is all about \"bargaining down the contractor as low as possible.\"  I believe in paying fairly for someone's work.  I just don't know what would be reasonable now.  If I were to pay someone $120,000 for this small add-on, it would be financially irresponsible.  I'm in a modest neighborhood, and I would be investing far outside what I could reasonably expect to get for my home--even in this tight market.  Any thoughts on this would be appreciated.  At this point, I feel almost embarrassed to call anyone else with my apparently paltry budget.  Thank you for any light you can shed.  I appreciate it.", "images": []}

Der Garten hat rund 90m2 Fl\u00e4che und grenzt an 3 Nachbargrundst\u00fccke mit H\u00f6hendifferenzen von -1m bis +2m gegen\u00fcber unserem Grundst\u00fcck an. Aktuell befinden sich darauf neben einer Rasenfl\u00e4che zwei kleine Steinterrassen sowie als Sichtschutz Hecken, darunter eine Thujahecke mit 3,5m H\u00f6he als Sichtschutz gegen\u00fcber einem Nachbargrundst\u00fcck, das 2m \u00fcber unserem Grundst\u00fcck liegt. Was uns an dem aktuellen Garten nicht gef\u00e4llt: - Blick auf die \"Thujawand\" von der Hauptterrasse (Terrasse 1) aus - extrem viel Platzverlust durch Thujahecke (1,5m breit; leider kann die Hecke nicht schm\u00e4ler geschnitten werden, da sie unter der ersten Astschicht bereits braun ist) - geringer Sichtschutz durch die seitlichen Hecken - unansehliche Pflanzsteine zum H\u00f6henausgleich, in denen trotz flei\u00dfigem Gie\u00dfen so gut wie alles eingeht - neben der Hecke wenig andere Pflanzen Die bisherigen \u00dcberlegungen: - Aufgrund des H\u00f6henunterschieds zum Nachbarn werden wir wohl die Thujahecke - trotz der Tatsache, dass sie mit einer Tiefe von 1,5m enorm viel Platz in dem kleinen Garten einnimmt - beibehalten m\u00fcssen (> Solltet ihr eine Alternative haben, die uns kurzfristig einen vergleichbaren Sichtschutz in der H\u00f6he bietet, w\u00e4ren wir hier\u00fcber sehr dankbar.) - Um den Blick aber auf etwas sch\u00f6neres zu lenken, wollten wir eine der beiden Terrasse erh\u00f6ht in die Grundst\u00fccksecke verlegen. title: Skip laurel, cherry laurel or wax myrtle for Zone 7a hedging? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "smalloldhouse-gw", "author_name": "smalloldhouse_gw", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/smalloldhouse-gw", "date": "2022-02-16", "text": "I am hoping to install some hedging to give a better sense of separation between my house and my neighbor. I sought advice from a nursery which recommended skip laurels (prunus laurocerasus). Based on the app that I've been using to ID shrubs that others in my neighborhood use for a similar purpose, many many people seem to use cherry laurels (prunus caroliniana.) Btw please don't flame me if I've got the distinction here wrong: a lot of googling hasn't helped me really understand if there is a real difference between these two! Meanwhile, on a local message board, someone recommended using wax myrtle (myrica cerifera) instead of laurels, noting that skip laurels are prone to fungus and that wax myrtle grows more densely. I'm wondering if anyone here can help me decide which direction to take? I'm located a mile or two north of Washington DC and I'm planting in full sun (with a giant old water oak about 25 feet away that provides a bit of screening from the worst of the summer sun.) Thank you!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "dave-in_nova", "author_name": "Dave in NoVA \u2022 N. Virginia \u2022 zone 7A", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dave-in_nova", "date": "2022-02-19", "text": "You didn't say how high your hedge needs to be.  Are deer a problem? How's the drainage? No for Prunus caroliniana. It is a tree and can get damaged in winter. But there may be other Prunus such as Skip laurel, provided they get enough moisture. It can get 8 to 15 feet. Prunus laurocerasus 'Otto Luyken' works for many years. Doesn't get much over 4 or 5 feet. But can eventually get white scale and die out. Euonymus is great provided your area is fenced from deer. Golden euonymus, Silver King euonymus, etc. Wax myrtle may work, but can defoliate in really cold winters. Also, snow loads can break them up, which is discouraging, but deer don't like them. You might consider Viburnum pragense. It's a bit course, but with shaping looks fairly good. Takes regular maintenance. Stays evergreen. It's tough and deer don't care for it.  Leaves droop in coldest weather. Then there are all the hollies, such as I cornuta 'Burford', 'Needlepoint', 'Carissa', I. cornuta Rotundifolia, Ilex crenata and all it's cultivars, the Blue hollies and all their cultivars.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "gaf-ml_01", "author_name": "Rose Beginner(MA - 6A)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gaf-ml_01", "date": "2022-02-16", "text": "Our roof is over 20 years old and due for replacement.  We\u2019ve noticed some leaks, and therefore want the a rubber membrane replaced (or installed; we don\u2019t know for sure if there is one there already).  Here in New England, ice dams are a regular problem. One roofer suggests send the membrane up to the peak, but not over it.  He\u2019ll install a new ridge vent.  The other says it\u2019s a bad idea to do the entire roof like that, suggesting instead sening the membrane up either 6\u2019 or 9\u2019, and using a thick underlayment (something akin to Tyvek but thicker; is that roofing felt?) for the rest. Any opinions on which roofer is right?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "millworkman", "author_name": "millworkman", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/millworkman", "date": "2022-02-16", "text": "Typically an Ice & Water Barrier would be run the entire roof surface, stopping just shy of the ridge to allow for the ridge vent.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "3onthetree", "author_name": "3onthetree", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3onthetree", "date": "2022-02-17", "text": "An ice barrier is required to be installed from the edge of eave to a point 24\" inside the exterior wall line. Since the roll is 36\" wide, usually a roofer will lay just one row and stop no matter the eave length. Another row might be beneficial and more exact to code, but since the self-stick ice barrier is very difficult to get off in the future, it is typically not installed all the way up to ridge. And there usually aren't roof leaks in the blank field of a roof; they mostly occur at penetrations and transitions, so the ice barrier over the entire roof plane may not help in any leak prevention anyway. title: Worm Castings - Beneficial or Not | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "a1an", "author_name": "a1an", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/a1an", "date": "2022-02-16", "text": "Did a impulse buy as I walked buy and spied a bag of worm castings. Upon getting home and gathering my thoughts, the initial app for it was to put it into new potting mix for some new plantings. I think it may make the -mix- too mush, and I should just stick with liquids...... Which then leads to what do I do with this bag 'ole bag of castings. Sigh. I guess I can just bring it back on the next go around. I mean the -stuff in dirt- has got plenty of castings already....", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2022-02-20", "text": "There is nothing in worm castings in the way of nutrition that can't be found in fertilizer, and not only is there no chance it will improve a container mediums structure, as it's fine texture will be detrimental to any medium that is appropriate for conventional container growing. How detrimental is directly related to how much is used. About mycorrhizae - A) Pots generally offer inhospitable conditions that aren't conducive to the long-term survival of fungi that are capable of forming symbiotic relationships with plants they share the pot with. Populations  of beneficial fungi tend toward boom/bust at best. E.g., when I repot in early spring or occasionally in late fall, or when I check roots in  winter by tipping the plant out of the pot to examine roots, the pots  are generally well-populated with of hyphae of a variety of fungi. Once  summer temps and sunshine (sunlight striking the pot and creating heat) come into play, the fungi seem to vanish until temps cool again. I can't  imagine that indoor conditions would be any better. Almost all the  temperate plants I grow are passively inoculated by beneficial fungi spores which arrive on the wind, and the fungi proliferate under influence of cool/cold temps, but I've  never seen the fungi or evidence thereof in a planting that has been growing indoors. B) All else equal, plants in pots that DO form relationships with beneficial fungi do not need a root system as large as plants that do not form the relationships. Plants are very economical, so if they don't need a larger root system they will not grow it. This means that if something occurs suddenly that reduces the population of fungal pals (like application of a fungicide or other  product not appreciated by the fungal friendlies, the root system very  suddenly becomes much too small to support the top of the plant, which  can cause serious consequences. This is the primary reason I choose not to court growth of friendly fungi in pots. At least for the way I grow,  their cultural wants are well beyond what I'm willing to do to try to keep them thriving. I'm growing plants, not fungi. Be very careful about holding great expectations for products claiming to contain live mycorrhizae. It takes very little heat to kill packaged/living fungi. Some products will contain some live fungi and some none. Some will contain fungi that are unable to live in or adapt to the cultural conditions under which we expect them to prove beneficial. As a variation on the theme \"if you build it, they will come\", if we establish a container planting and the conditions in the container are conducive to establishment of beneficial fungi, they will arrive and establish quickly w/o our help. Al", "images": []}}

title: Passive House en el Maresme | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "sigla-studio-pfvwes-pf~28583155", "author_name": "SIGLA STUDIO", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/design-build-firms/sigla-studio-pfvwes-pf~28583155", "date": "2022-02-17", "text": "El proyecto trata la nueva construcci\u00f3n de una vivienda unifamiliar aislada. El edificio se proyecta a cuatro vientos manteniendo una relaci\u00f3n formal con el solar. Consiste en una planta rectangular ortogonal, con la fachada este y oeste paralelas a los limites del solar y retirada del limite sur para poder ubicar una importante extension de jard\u00edn con piscina. Para resolver la singular pendiente del solar se proyecta un talud escalonado construido en tres niveles, adaptando cada nivel a un uso. Siendo el nivel mas alto una extensi\u00f3n de c\u00e9sped, seguido de un nivel completamente ocupado por la piscina, y por ultimo, al mismo nivel de la calle, una extension de gravas.   Al tratarse de una passive house, el programa adem\u00e1s considera su implantaci\u00f3n en relaci\u00f3n al entorno y sit\u00faa los espacios y estancias principales en la fachada sur. Estas se relacionan con el exterior mediante espacios intermedios, un porche a lo largo de toda la fachada en la planta baja y dos terrazas situadas en la planta primera. Por un lado, la planta baja resuelve todas las necesidades de una vivienda sin necesidad de contar con la planta piso. Consta de un sal\u00f3n, comedor y cocina que comparten un solo ambiente, una habitaci\u00f3n polivalente con las dimensiones de una habitaci\u00f3n doble, un ba\u00f1o completo y un lavadero. En la planta piso se encuentran 3 habitaciones dobles y dos ba\u00f1os completos.   El dise\u00f1o reticular y completamente sim\u00e9trico de la vivienda permiten la entrada de luz natural tanto en el sal\u00f3n como en las estancias principales as\u00ed como la ventilaci\u00f3n cruzada desde todas las fachadas. Al mismo tiempo, se implantan unas persianas correderas en la fachada con la intenci\u00f3n de ampliar las ventanas y aberturas.   Esta vivienda de alta eficiencia energ\u00e9tica y bajo mantenimiento se ha resuelto con soluciones singulares en cuanto a su materializaci\u00f3n. En el exterior, se utiliza el ladrillo como material protagonista jugando con distintos tipos de aparejo que se adaptan a la arquitectura. En el interior se emplean otros materiales naturales como la madera abedul, piedra cenia en pavimentos de ba\u00f1os y toda la planta baja, y moqueta de fibra de yute en las habitaciones de la planta piso.   Tanto en el exterior como en el interior se aplica una est\u00e9tica monocrom\u00e1tica, predominando los tonos rojizos en el exterior, en contraste con el blanco y beige del interior de la vivienda que dotan de continuidad y atemporalidad a los espacios.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/2e11abfd01ee7273_1298-w500-h442-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/c461ab8a01ee727d_1298-w500-h333-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/e591890801ee7280_4125-w500-h466-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/43e1f21001ee7284_2736-w500-h393-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/30a1138901ee726f_1298-w500-h448-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/6561bdec01ee7278_1298-w500-h442-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: Gas Furnace/Attic Insualtion | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-89385627", "author_name": "Luna Tonks", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-89385627", "date": "2022-02-17", "text": "So, I have a gas furnace and the upstairs unit is in the attic.  There is about a 2 foot by 2 foot square around the plenum of the furnace that communicates straight down from attic to the second floor.  The furnace itself sits in an interior closet and the plenum is probably 1 foot x 1 foot.  I am planning on blowing more insulation into the attic.  The insulation in there is gnarly to say the least. . However, I feel like no matter what I do, that hole is going to be an issue.  If its hot outside, its hot upstairs.  The AC will chill the upstairs, but as soon as you turn it off, it starts to get hot again. I know the furnace needs air to breath and get a good combustion.  My thought was to put plywood from the attic floor to the plenum, then add batting.  That would let the furnace get fresh air, but also keep the hot/cold air from the attic from going straight down to the 2nd story.  I have reservations about plywood being close to the combustion pipe. Obviously, spray foam would be the best option, but it's not feasible with our budget and we are expecting our first child.  His room, and all bedrooms, are on the second floor.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~312471206", "author_name": "Austin Air Companie", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~312471206", "date": "2022-02-18", "text": "Luna Tonks, The flue pipe you show is not a combustion pipe. That is a flue pipe. Combustion air is not drawn from a flue pipe it is drawn from fresh air around the appliance, in this case that air is drawn from the attic which is why the attic space around the plenum that sticks up into the attic is open. If gas furnaces do not have proper combustion air this results in incomplete combustion and produces large amounts of CO or carbon monoxide. Gas furnaces are not a DIY appliance. There are safety concerns to be considered. Do not attempt to seal that cavity up from the attic, it is there for a reason. title: Preferred grass for Woodland Hills, CA  north face lawn some shade? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "mystrwizard", "author_name": "mystrwizard", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mystrwizard", "date": "2022-02-17", "text": "We have an area (about 500 sq. ft) currently of fescue that is worn out and dead in a lot of spots, wanted to repair or replace. There is a tree over part of the lawn, a Chinese Pistache that is very thick in summer shading probably half of the lawn in mid-day but grass would get sun in morning and afternoon while the other part of the lawn gets sun all day long in summer but in winter due to 2-story house, this lawn gets no direct sun except early morning.  The Pistache does loose all its leaves in winter.  Area does not get alot of traffic, no kids but two small dogs (indoor) that do enjoy this lawn during parts of the day. Any ideas would be greatly appreciated. James", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "dchall-san_antonio", "author_name": "dchall_san_antonio", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dchall-san_antonio", "date": "2022-02-18", "text": "I'm not sure there's a perfectly responsible answer to this because of the drought; however, fescue is definitely NOT an answer.  The reason you have bare spots in the fescue is that once a fescue plant is damaged enough, it dies and does not come back.  It takes periodic overseeding, often annually (in the late summer), to keep fescue looking really nice.  If you lived in El Segundo or one of the foggy morning beachfront cities, you might get away with fescue.  Lake Arrowhead would work for fescue because of the summer cool temps, but you are down in the relatively dry heat. The only warm season grass that will work in the shade is St Augustine.  It can take a lot of shade and still look nice.  It does well in full sun and becomes very dense, but shade is fine.  Rather than recommend some variety that you cannot get locally, I'd suggest you call some of the nurseries around to see what they carry.  See if you can find a nursery where the local landscapers buy.  We have one in San Antonio where you can buy individual pieces of St Augustine sod for $1.75, whereas the price is $2.99 at HD and Lowes.  Furthermore the nursery sells 14 pallets per day while HD and Lowes sells maybe 5 pallets per week.  So the nursery sod is guaranteed fresh and the box stores is guaranteed diseased.  Once you get the grass, it must be installed the same day to keep if from overnighting under other grass and getting the disease. Unlike fescue, St Augustine goes dormant in the winter when the temps drop below freezing.  It returns in March.  Some people overseed with 'winter rye' to keep something green all year, but I always advise against that.  The winter rye provides enough shade on the dormant St Aug in the spring that awakening is delayed by 4-6 weeks.  After a delayed awakening the grass seems to struggle the rest of the season. Mow St Aug at the mower's highest setting all the time.  In the shade there is never a reason to scalp it down.  In full sun, after many years, you might want to scalp it in the summer to reduce the density.  I like to mow mine every 2 weeks to keep it tall.  Tall St Augustine tends to prevent weeds and other grasses from growing.", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "julieste", "author_name": "julieste", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/julieste", "date": "2022-02-18", "text": "Photos of your current space would help. We're getting close to the end of a complete gut remodel of a condo kitchen close to the same size as yours except ours is a bit smaller (ours is 9 x 13). Although ours is a different set-up, I had many of the same complaints you have. Ours is a U configuration (as in your new plan) set up with sink, range and fridge on the same walls as your plan. And, there are just two of us. After MUCH deliberation we went with a plan that has super susans in both corners (love them a lot and so glad we went with that option). Our sink is in the same spot as yours, but the dishwasher is to the right of the sink, and that helps to really open up the range corner.  (In the past, both of us were trying to crowd into that one corner by the range to cook and load/unload dishwasher.) We have an interior kitchen with no natural light at all. We did lots of can lighting AND we opened up two large, 5' wide by 3 high \"window\" pass throughs (one on the sink wall and one on the fridge wall.) The kitchen how has both a sense of enclosure and a sense of openness at the same time. Trimming out the \"windows\" creates a much more finished appearance rather than just having a rectangular hole cut on the sheetrock. I question the little bar/sitting space you have at the end  of the cabinet run and whether it's really worthwhile. Rather than centering it, I would think about moving the fridge as far to the end of that wall as possible without interfering with the window. Then put a small counter section under the window next to it so you will have a landing spot. This would give you much more uninterrupted working space near the range. As regards the fridge, I should also say that we went with a regular depth fridge rather than listening to the standard advice here which is to always go with a counter depth for a better appearance. We boxed the fridge in with side panels, and it gives the appearance of a somewhat separate fridge niche rather than just having a huge fridge stick out.  We have no other space a second fridge, bar fridge or mini fridge so need to have as much fridge space as possible. We are happy with the extra fridge space a regular depth fridge gives us. Since we put it at the end of a run (except for a narrow pull out pantry between the wall and the fridge), it doesn't appear to be overly  obtrusive.", "images": []}}

title: Deep thoughts......The ethics of curiosity. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "amylou321", "author_name": "amylou321", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/amylou321", "date": "2022-02-17", "text": "I was watching a documentary series about ancient Egypt, something I enjoy. I like history, especially ancient history. However, something struck me. One of the episodes of the series was dedicated to \"tomb raiders.\" Of course, these people were portrayed as negative. Thieves, grave robbers, low lifes. I do not fully disagree. HOWEVER, I couldn't help but wonder, what do you call modern day archeologists and scientists who are digging these people up and putting them on display to he public, or worse, boxing them up to be left on a shelf or in a drawer? What about in the case of King Tut, whose treasures were still in his tomb, only to be taken in the name of science, and put on display to bring in tourists to gawk. You still robbed his tomb. These ancient tomb raiders were stealing treasures from tombs for monetary gain. Is it better or worse to take them to satisfy the urge to learn about a culture long gone? In the case of Egypt, the people they are hauling out of their graves specifically built their tombs to keep their remains safe for eternity. They truly believed that their earthly remains and all their goods were an absolute requirement for their afterlife. Is it okay to disrespect that now because most people no longer subscribe to that? I admit I LOVED seeing the tomb of Queen Nefertari on the documentary series. It was so beautiful and fascinating to think that all that work and detail was put into a structure that was never meant to be seen by human eyes again. But I was sad that when it was discovered, all that was left was her mummified legs and a pair of reed sandals. And as I watched the historian talk about how her tomb was sacked, I couldn't help but wonder if he was angry at the desecration of her tomb, or was he mad that they got there first, before WE could see it, pick through it, and keep it for ourselves in a museum or institution somewhere. It not just ancient Egypt of course. I just used them as an example because the documentary was what got me thinking about it. Of course people from all sorts of cultures have been dug up, poked and prodded so that we modern people can learn about them. All in all, I am torn. I enjoy learning about ancient people, their lives and cultures. I would like to think that they would not have liked to be forgotten, though I could be wrong.  But I also dislike the processes necessary to obtain such information. And I really really do not like the fact that mummies and other remains are put on display to the public. These were real people! I would NOT like to have my remains gawked at by casually curious people centuries from now.  In the end, do we NEED to know about them at all? Is there something in these remains that could prove beneficial to us now? Or is it just a want to know situation? What are your thoughts?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "elmerjfudd", "author_name": "Elmer J Fudd", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/elmerjfudd", "date": "2022-02-18", "text": "Legitimate archaeologists, Egyptologists and the like are academics who study, explore and analyze the artifacts and places of ancient peoples. Expanding our knowledge and understanding of people who lived long ago add to our collective understanding of the past and present. There's no reason to feel melancholy or sentimental about what they do. This is to be contrasted with looters and others who plunder such items for personal gain or benefit. The religious extremist family that owns Hobby Lobby has been caught numerous times buying ancient items of questionable or no provenance that could only have been items stolen or looted. These are the scoundrels to speak up against, not the academics doing legitimate scholarship. Without such people of questionable ethics and morals willing to buy anything from anyone (which museums and honest collectors refuse to do), there would be no markets for stolen and looted items.", "images": []}}

title: Loft conversion and upper floor layout thoughts | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "ewan-jobe", "author_name": "Ewan Jobe", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ewan-jobe", "date": "2022-02-18", "text": "The background I\u2019d like to start out by saying that obviously we will be seeking the services of a structural engineer. I know how many threads like this get posted by people looking for an easy out. I\u2019m just here mainly to write out my thoughts and hopefully get some pointers and opinions so I know what to ask them. We moved into this house about a year ago, knowing it would need some work. I had hoped that the roof would last another winter and we could get it sorted this summer, but Storm Arwen had other ideas and left us with a significant hole of missing slates on one side. We managed to get it patched, but successive storms have further taken their toll and pushed it up the priority list.   Obviously we could just get it replaced as is, but that seems like a big wasted opportunity when, if we\u2019re going through all the trouble, we could get a lot of things in place for a conversion and end up with an extra room at the end of it. The house It\u2019s mid terrace, c. 1890s with solid wall construction \u2013 albeit chunky ones that measure about 15\u201d/40cm thick. Originally it was likely just a one up one down, but there\u2019s a 3.8m single storey extension to the rear with the kitchen and a small box room. The upper floor has been split up to accommodate the bathroom, but the living room is still just one large room, approx 5.4m squared. There\u2019s a stud wall to enclose the staircase but nothing structural. The roof is supported by a king post, with two separate purlins on each side. Pitch is around 39 degrees, with head height in the centre of the loft being 2.38m. We paid around 60k for the house just after the first lockdown (we\u2019re in the North East), although similar houses are currently going for around 80k. So while we don\u2019t have any plans to sell in the immediate future, it doesn\u2019t make much sense to go all out on a high end 30k conversion. We will be contracting the shell of the structure and obviously the electrics, and DIYing as much of the rest as possible. I have enough experience of plastering and joinery to get by. One thing we are blessed by in this house is high ceilings, 3.2m on the ground floor and 2.9m on the upper floor. So whichever option we go for I would be very tempted to lower the ceiling to around 2.6m, increase the head height in the conversion and also give us the opportunity to board it out before removing the old lath and plaster, minimising disruption to the bedroom below. Presumably this would necessitate some kind of tie between the rafter ends and the lower joists to transfer the horizontal load of the roof. Conventional wisdom is that the best place for a staircase to the loft conversion is right above the existing one. However, there are a few quirks of this house that are making me think that this may not be the case here. This is the layout of the upper floor currently:   So a staircase above the existing one would take up about 2m of space from the current master bedroom. 860 mm for the staircase, 900 for a hallway, plus a bit for the stud walls and plasterboard. Compounding this, if we ever wanted to extend above the kitchen, the door into that extension would have to be roughly where the bathroom sink currently is, removing at least 1m of space from the bathroom. So we could end up in a weird situation where nearly half of the space on the upper floor is taken up by passageways, and the main bathroom of the house is a small box room with no windows.   The alternative I have in mind is moving the bathroom into that space with the boiler in the top right, adding a new window, running the staircase up where the bathroom currently is in front of the chimney breast, and reclaiming some length into the bedroom as well as some under stair storage. This might present some difficulties plumbing wise, but I believe it\u2019s been done in quite a few houses in the street looking at the number of additional small windows in the front. This would look something like this:   The options Given that there is only 5.4m between the front and back walls, I was pondering the possibility of a conversion that neither uses steels, nor impacts on the party walls at all. Going by the span tables on the NHBC website this would just about be possible using 75 x 220 C24 timber. In fact this is how the upper floor joists currently run. We just may need to replace the timber lintels on the inner leaf for the windows on these walls. I fear that supporting the roof from this floor using purlin walls would probably push it above the 0.5 kN/m\u00b2 dead load limit, but given that the rafters only span about 3.5m from the wall plate to the ridge board, it should be possible to replace them with 170 mm C16 timber and have them unsupported along the entire span. This would give us a lot of depth for insulation as well, and we may even be able to use rockwool instead of PIR. My only question with this is how would the upgraded rafters be attached in such a way that maintains the existing roof pitch, given that the birds mouth would have to go much more than 1/3 of the way through the thickness of the timber. I guess the wall plate would have to be lowered by a course of bricks or two? Clearly this solution uses a lot of quite expensive (and heavy) timbers, but cost wise is still fairly favourable compared to using three section steels and smaller timbers. I estimate around 1100 for the floor joists and ledger boards, and around 700 for the new rafters. The main disadvantage of this option is that even with dropped ceilings, you would only have full head height along the centre of the room, and without a ridge beam supported on the party walls we\u2019d likely be limited to velux style windows mirrored on each side to balance out the load. Maybe there\u2019s some way to have a small dormer with a timber ridge beam supported on stud walls, but that\u2019s a question for the SE. The other option is to have a dormer to the rear of the property, which has already been done by someone a bit further down the street. Obviously this would require at least one steel at the ridge, although it may make sense to have another for the floor as well at that point. A steel on one side of the chimney breast would limit the longest span to around 3.6m, which would only require 145/170mm timbers. This would give you a lot more room to walk around in the conversion, although head height may still be quite limited with the drop down from the ridge, and insulation required for a warm roof construction. The steels would impart a not insignificant additional cost, as would the labour of installing them and the more complex joinery required. We would have to seek a party wall award, as well as the additional charge for the building inspector. I will use a 73\" (top measurement)  double sink vanity on the 77.5\" wall. The sinks are 17.5\" long, and the space  from the sink to the end of the top is 7\". I would like to use a recessed mirrored medicine cabinet on top  of each sink, with sconces on each outside side of the mirror and one in the center, between the two mirrors. I saw a 24\"W x 30\"L mirror with LED lights on the front. The only other light in the bathroom is inside the shower, which is on the opposite side of the vanity, running open (with glass) the whole 77.5\" wall. My questions are: A) Will the outside sconces be too tight between the mirror and side wall? B) Should I use a  light fixture above the mirrors, instead of the side sconces? C) Am I going to need light fixtures, if I use the mirrored medicine cabinets with the LED light? Remember that the only other light in the bathroom is on the opposite wall (shower light) . Thank you!", "images": []}

{"Comment 1": {"author_id": "wdccruise", "author_name": "wdccruise", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/wdccruise", "date": "2022-02-19", "text": "
  • The distance between the vanity and the wall is ( 77.5" - 73" ) / 2 = 2.25"
  • The centerline of a sink is ( 17.5" / 2 ) + 7" + 2.25" = 18" from the wall.

  • If centered, you'd have a sconce 8.25" / 2 = 4.125" from the outside edge of the mirror.
  • You will have 77.5" - ( 8.25" x 2 ) - ( 24" x 2 ) = 13" between the mirrors.

main_question: {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2022-02-19", "text": "I took some cuttings of marjoram last year in a big pot, and got an excellent crop. It kinda died in the winter, which I thought to be odd because allegedly marjoram can tolerate light frosts. I barely had even that. I kept replanting in the pot, throughout the winter, and it kept dying, even though I protected it from even light freezes. Then either turn off the appliance until all the ice has melted completely (this can take a surprisingly long time), or use a hair dryer to accelerate the process. The reason why I tell you to remove the cover for the coils is that you have to make sure they are completely free of ice, and with the cover in place there really is no good way to reliably tell that. I don't know anything about your specific model, but I have learned that there often are very instructive videos on Youtube showing you how to service your own appliances. title: Help choosing a water softener | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "brian-ho59", "author_name": "Brian Ho", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/brian-ho59", "date": "2022-02-19", "text": "I got quotes from 3 different companies that are all comparable but are offering different systems: Clack, Puronics, and Hague. Anyone have any ideas as to how to these compare in terms of long term maintenance costs? All reviews online seem to be from extremely biased sources.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-867564120", "author_name": "HU-867564120", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-867564120", "date": "2022-02-19", "text": "I wouldn't hesitate to go with the Clack system, the company was started by ex-Fleck engineers, so they know what they are doing. Very reliable, well thought out design. No issues in 15 years with our Clack unit.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2022-02-19", "text": "Systems that are based on Clack or Fleck control valves are very reliable. Fleck based systems are available over the internet whereas Clack has prohibited internet sales. For that reason, Fleck based systems tend to be less expensive and more common. If what you are trying to do is remove hardness, you don't need $5,000 worth of equipment. Water softening is a commodity business. There's no \"special sauce\" that makes water \"more soft\". Buy a SOFTENER - not a conditioner or anything like that. If you can get one that uses a Clack or Fleck valve - that's good. I've often talked about $600-700 Fleck based softeners on Amazon (softener only, no install, sizing, etc). The point is that the actual cost of just the hardware should be under $1,000 for a decent softener. The rest of the value comes from the dealer doing a good job of testing the water, sizing it properly, installing it and configuring it.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "brian-ho59", "author_name": "Brian Ho", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/brian-ho59", "date": "2022-02-20", "text": "Any opinion on Hague?", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2022-02-20", "text": "Just quickly reading about them: They make all their stuff - including the control valve. I would stick with Clack or Fleck control valves. The control valve is THE heart of the softener - it's the mechanical part that will go bad (besides the resin that will deteriorate over 12-15 years). That's why we are talking about the control valve. Don't do anything else with the water softener - no carbon, for example - if you want a carbon filter, do that separately. You don't want to mix media inside the water softener. Again, the water softener is pretty straightforward and other than getting a decent control valve, there's not a lot to differentiate one from the other.", "images": []}}

title: replacing old radiators | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-188464289", "author_name": "Vince C", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-188464289", "date": "2022-02-20", "text": "Looking for opinions and advice here. I am looking to replace some really old radiators in the house but found out that the width of it is 1270mm, which does not really fit the convector heaters or column radiator widths that I could find. Is the design solution to use valve extensions with a 1200mm radiator (closest size I could find) or really have to take up the floorboards and move the copper pipes underneath.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jonathandb1972", "author_name": "Jonathan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jonathandb1972", "date": "2022-02-20", "text": "Get the radiator size that is right for the room and then move the pipes accordingly. Old radiators had to be wide to heat the room but many newer more efficient radiators take up less space. Go online and find a BTU calculator.   You enter the size of the room and it will calculate how powerful the radiator needs to be. You can then plan the ideal size and might even find that in some rooms you can reduce from two to only one radiator and therefore gain wall space.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "feature-radiators", "author_name": "Feature Radiators", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/feature-radiators", "date": "2022-07-01", "text": "Hi Vince, you could look at a column radiator, for example we have a steel column radiator called the Core, we can add individual sections on until we reach close to the width of your existing radiator. If you cannot move the pipework you would need to measure from the centre of one pipe to the centre of the other, then we would help to find a radiator and valves (and maybe extensions) to hit as close as possible to the existing pipework. As the previous person mentioned though, it is worth checking the heat output requirement as it can often cost more to try to fit existing pipe centres than just actually moving the pipework as you could be oversizing for the room. Give us a call, we would be happy to help - 01274 567789.", "images": []}}

title: Favorite rugosa | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "yuliya-mi", "author_name": "Yulia_6a_Michigan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/yuliya-mi", "date": "2022-02-20", "text": "Hi guys,I am putting fenced vegetable garden and will have landscaping done around it to make it look nice. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "oldmoses", "author_name": "Moses, Pitt PA, cold W & hot-humid S, z6", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/oldmoses", "date": "2022-02-22", "text": "Roseraie de L' Hay- for a tall bush, 4'-5'.  Best flower formed larger blooming Hybrid Rugosa there is, IMHO.  Few to no hips,  consequently it's a v.g. rebloomer. Snow Pavement (Schnee Koppe, Ger.), for a medium height 36\" - 40\", very pale pink/mauve, nicely cupped blooms. Not many cupped Hybrid Rugosas, most are flat, disheveled, ' blown-up looking' blooms with confused centers. Henry Hudson - best shorter HR, at 30\",  heavily petaled, 2.5\" - 3\" snow white blooms with an occasional lightest pink tinge.  The best formed flower of any Hybrid Rugosa I grew. These are my 3 favorite Hybrid Rugosas. Grow tested about 30 different Hybrid Rugosa varities....some were real dogs! Never spray anything onto Hybrid Rugosa foliage.  That includes Neem oil, insecticidal soap, foliar spray fertilizer, or foliar spray fungicide.  The foliage will burn and drop. Some hot dry summers, spider mites can be a problem with Hybrid Rugosas.  Just let nature take it's course since spraying is not an option both from your veggie garden standpoint, and the foliage damage inevitability if sprayed.  A soil drench miticide will work for mites, but not near veggies. Hydrangea Little Lime, at 3-4', or even Hydrangea Bobo, at 2-3', may be better heights outside your vegetable garden fence.  H. Limelight can get to 6-8' easily.  Give the smaller hydrangeas  consideration. Moses", "images": []}}

The current house floor space is ~230m2, single story, orientation is easterly, double brick build, built on foundations (not a slab). Build circa 1965. The condition of the stuff that matters ie; foundations, brick work, floor joists is excellent from a visual inspection - no signs of brick work cracking, efflorescence on bricks and it has those wonderful never to be seen again hardwood floor joists (you builders out there know what I am talking about - great color, dense grain and straight as a tack), interior walls all brick. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mongoct", "author_name": "MongoCT", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mongoct", "date": "2022-02-20", "text": "Gypsum board has been prohibited since the 2006 code revision as a tile backer board in wet areas like showers. Meaning you can't bond tile directly to the gypsum board. Doesn't matter if it is plain ole gypsum board or moisture resistant gypsum board. There are surface applied membranes (Kerdi for example) where the manufacturer of Kerdi allows Kerdi to be applied directly to gypsum board. Now it's fine that Schluter allows it, but even after all these years there are still some AHJs that don't allow it. When using a surface applied membrane (liquid or sheet) often the safest approach...and the most sensible...is to apply the SAM over cement board. Liquid membranes need to be applied to a specific minimum thickness for them to be able to provide waterproofing to the substrate behind it. Will they use a mil thickness gauge? Or guess? As Mark mentioned in the previous post, ask your builder what the construction/waterproofing sequence will be for the shower. Also for the shower floor. If using something like an Oatey membrane, code requires the floor membrane itself to be sloped to the drain. It's a code violation to install the membrane flat on the subfloor and simply install sloped mud and tile on top of the flat membrane. Don't forget to ask about the shower ceiling. main_question: {"author_id": "dr-benjamin-cohen-pfvwus-pf~1350645403", "author_name": "Dr Benjamin Cohen", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/interior-designers-and-decorators/dr-benjamin-cohen-pfvwus-pf~1350645403", "date": "2022-02-20", "text": "Looking for 48\" range hood that is efficient (> 600 CFM) while relatively quiet. Most seem to be rated as \"noisy\".  Is it true that you can insert a fan silencer in all ducted units?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2022-02-20", "text": "When the blower used with a hood is remote from the hood, whether in-line in the duct path or outdoors on roof or wall, and there is enough length and diameter to fit it, then a silencer can be added that will remove almost all blade tip turbulence noise generated by the blower.  Such silencers look like truck mufflers and are available from Fantech.  Baffle noise, duct noise on the hood side of the silencer, and any flow transition induced noises are not affected, but these tend to not dominate the noise as the blade tip turbulence does. So whenever feasible, use remote blowers with large hoods needing high flow rates to achieve the needed air velocity at the baffles. If your hood is, say four feet by two feet in entry area, then I recommend 8 sq. ft. x 90 ft./s = 720 CFM actual flow, which will require a 1000 - 1200 CFM rated blower.  You will also need a make-up air system. Please review as many hood and MUA threads on this forum as you can fit into your time to gain perspective of the technical, space, and financial costs of addressing pro-style cooking appliance needs.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "994house", "author_name": "994house", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/994house", "date": "2022-02-20", "text": "Hi!We understand the benefits of induction cooking. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2022-02-20", "text": "While induction cooking lacks the added gas combustion products in the cooking plume, the cooking plume still expands as it rises.  This is the rationale for wider and deeper hoods than have been historically used in kitchens.  But best is the enemy of good enough, and good enough depends on configuration of cabinets, burners/hobs used for grease and moisture laden cooking effluent -- middle or boundary, cross drafts, and other effects. There are a lot of ways to transport grease into the air without frying or searing, so frying rarity may not be a good reason for not going wider.  It is more of an architectural issue in already existing kitchens than a \"we don't need it because ...\" issue.  Wider does have various increased costs associated with it, but I won't belabor this paragraph touching on them.  Please review the many hood and make-up air related threads on this forum for perspective and references. This forum is littered from more than a decade ago with commentaries supporting induction and, conversely, gas.  Induction wins on safety, ease of cooktop surface cleaning, low heat warming (chocolate is not just for breakfast anymore) and other cooking that can make use of its wide \"dynamic range\" (full power to minimum power), less heat in the kitchen in summer, and other factors I've forgotten.  Safety includes no gas risk, and lower surface temperatures than with other electrical or gas cooking approaches. Negatives are no roasting of peppers over the burner, need for inductive base pots and pans, significantly more electrical power needed at the cooktop or range location, and theoretical and experiential lower long term reliability due to electronic complexity, although this is improving, I think.", "images": []}}

title: Change engineer on approved permit? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "sanjose8899", "author_name": "S P", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/sanjose8899", "date": "2022-02-21", "text": "I hired a GC to get a permit for a whole house remodel. They hired subs (architect and structural engineer) to get the job done. (I know, I know I should have found my own\u2026lesson learned) The GC sent me the plans to review prior to submission to the city. It didn\u2019t include structural changes as he said they were being finished, but I didn\u2019t press on it since I assumed the engineer and GC knew what they were doing. After receiving the approved permits, I took a look at the structural plans and they make zero sense. My remodel is removing walls running parallel to the ceiling and floor joists of a 1 story house. The plan calls for a beam to be installed where each wall used to be. This doesn\u2019t make sense given the joists run parallel to the beams. I emailed the engineer directly to ask him and he said \u201coh I thought the joists went the other way. Where it 'lives' on the color wheel is over near the Yellow-Red hue family - this is where the perception of brown/brownish will come from - that is if it actually shows up as brownish. \"Brown\" is commonly a classification of dark orange. If it sat squarely in the Yellow-Red (orange) hue family there'd be no question you were gonna get brown. However, Urbane Bronze can also show up as greenish - because it is factually a dark Yellow, not dark orange. As we decrease the Chroma (colorfulness) in a Yellow hue family color, it gets cooler in temperature and that's where the green can come from. It all depends on the light and context as far as how it will actually show up. Which is why it's always best to test. Overtones and hue family are just as relevant to dark, low Chroma colors as they are to lighter and neutral colors. So, this is a great question. Iron Ore belongs to the Green-Yellow hue family. Light, mid tone and darker colors from the GY hue family are often perceived as being the most neutral. Meaning no discernible hue bias. Iron Ore will - likely - show up for most people as an off-black or very dark grayed charcoal. Nothing brownish about it. And despite technically belonging to a hue family that carries \"green\" in its name, Iron Ore is less likely to show moments of green than Urbane Bronze. Because of its hue family - AND - because it has a chunk less Chroma (colorfulness) Which also means Iron Ore is the more neutral in this comparison. We know all this because we have the factual numeric hue, value, chroma notations as a framework and can apply it for predicting how colors can actually show up in different light sources, in different contexts for different sets of eyeballs.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/d8c257f002141a2a_4593-w240-h135-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

title: You all dislike my kitchen layout. Help me figure it out :) | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "almostdone21", "author_name": "almostdone21", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/almostdone21", "date": "2022-02-22", "text": "I posted about which fridge I should choose for this layout and I got a lot of people saying the layout was bad and should be reconfigured. Here's the deal, what would you do given this kitchen size and constraints. (fyi anything is a major major upgrade because right now I have a bathroom in my kitchen, range in a tiny peninsula, and only one upper cabinet) - Can't move plumbing to the exterior wall where the range is, so the fridge can't go there -Can't move windows, so the sink must stay in the corner -Island is already as small as I would like to go 72\", needs to seat 3 children, so fridge can't go opposite on the other wall with the doorway or it would kill the island, and we will use that walkway to get to powder room so it will be high traffic over there. -We love the idea of having a dedicated coffee bar because we already have low counter space and I like to keep all the coffee stuff separate, but it's only 12\" deep in this layout because we are trying to give ample room for the pantry. -Need a decent-sized pantry for a family of 5. This one is 30\" and I can't imagine going any smaller, it will have pullouts inside. -This full-depth fridge in the pic will probably be replaced with a counter-depth one. - The mudroom, will possibly be a butlers pantry, or a coffee bar could go in there, but is that kinda weird to have your coffee made right off the powder room and too far from the fridge for creamer etc.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/1222a9c6021522e1_2353-w500-h359-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/fd82882902152259_2217-w500-h641-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/7f4298de0215225c_2239-w500-h500-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

Hoods over the cooking zone collect the rising and expanding cooking plume effluent that has high upward momentum.  Typical plumes of this sort result from frying, searing, and wok cooking.  Attempting to divert this flow of often significant plume CFM to the side (for a pop-up) or reversing the momentum to bring the plume to the counter (for a downdraft) is not practical for the apertures and flow rates that these downdraft schemes can implement at non-deafening flow rates.  Side-draft, and to a lesser degree down-draft schemes may work for low velocity plumes such as from slow simmering bacon and capturing vapor from a hot liquid surface. Cooking plumes from gas ranges can reach 1.2 m/s upward velocity.  A modest sized hot cooking* plume could be moving 240 CFM into the hood by itself.  Hood system air flow has to entrain this as well as any other plumes into the baffle filter, while assuring that plume components that hit metal and reflect typically downward are kept from escaping the flow. Also, the hood should overlap the cooking pans at the front as well as at the sides.  The key words for thinking about plume capture and containment are expanding and momentum. *(Hot cooking means at the vapor point of the oil used. title: Why are my bottle gourd seedlings dying? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "yaqing-cao", "author_name": "Eno", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/yaqing-cao", "date": "2022-02-22", "text": "This is my first year to grow bottle gourd. The seedlings emerged on 1/18. I moved them to outside several weeks later when the temp is around 68F (Bay Area). They were doing fine outside for a while. However, last week's temperature went down. And I decided to move them back inside my warm room. But they started to die one by one. The stems and leaves became soft and bend down first. Then the older leaves turned yellow and looked \"dehydrated\", while soil is still moist. I am going to start another batch of gourd seedlings again. But I am very confused about what exactly caused their deaths? Any help is appreciated!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/e3c26c44021570ba_2289-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/3b227ac6021570bc_2290-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "woodrose77", "author_name": "woodrose77", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/woodrose77", "date": "2022-02-24", "text": "I don't know exactly why your plants died, but it could be because they got too cold while outdoors. Gourds are a warm weather plant and don't like the cold at all. I don't know where you live, but it's way too early to start gourds here. Gourds can't be planted outside until all danger of frost is past and the weather stays warm. What kind of soil did you have your plants in ? The soil in the top pic looks pretty bad. It seems have a lot of salt buildup, and there appears to be a crusty ring of it around the base of the plant. Soil salinity may have had something to do with the death of your plants, but it's more likely they just got too cold. Next time, plant in a well-drained potting mix with no fertilizer and fill the pot almost full. Keep your plants where it's warm all the time until they are ready to be planted outside. When you transplant them try to not disturb their roots, they don't like that. Good luck with your next plants and I hope they grow and thrive !", "images": []}}
